speechtext:
On the order: Motions:
April 30, 1974-Mr. Fairweather-That the third report o£ the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, presented to the House on Tuesday, April 30, 1974, be concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal may gather, the Chair has had an opportunity to consider the terms of the report whose adoption he wishes to move at this time. I have to tell the hon. member and the House that in certain respects, in my view, the report as drafted contains terms which are absolutely without precedent in Canadian procedure and practice. I have no doubt whatsoever that the matter has been the subject of serious consideration by the Chairman and his advisers. I might mention in particular that the report, at least in appearance, seems to set up a new authority to authorize expenditure of public funds, an authority which is currently held by the Commissioners of Internal Economy by virtue of the House of Commons Act.
I want to be fair to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal. This is really a caution I am advancing at this time. I would like to have an opportunity to have a discussion with the hon. member for Fundy-Royal before we proceed with the motion. If the hon. member would agree, I would rather do it on this basis.

Mr. Speaker, wording for the report was suggested by officers of the House of Commons in a form which would allow our committee to have six law students employed should there be a dissolution of parliament. Although I have never been one who is particularly bothered by precedents, I did check with the government House leader and the House leader of the New Democratic Party and assumed there would be no trouble in employing these six students. However, if the motion is in terms that are not proper, I will take other advice.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I appreciate the comments made by the hon. member. I know how strongly he feels and how important it is to get the committee, of which he is a joint chairman, going. I am anxious to co-operate with him in this regard, but I do feel that in its present terms this report may cause some slight procedural difficulty in the future. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal will, I am sure,
not deny the Chair an opportunity to discuss the matter with him before the motion is put.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS PREPARED FOR CLAIMANTS BY INVESTIGATORY OFFICERS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. In view of present procedures whereby investigatory officers for the Unemployment Insurance Commission occasionally prepare statements for claimants in circumstances which call into question the voluntary nature and the accuracy of the information obtained, and which are often used to the detriment of the citizens concerned, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):

This practice does not appear to be followed in my constituency.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCTION IN GOVERNMENT CASH BALANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. With government cash balances down $1.5 billion in the last quarter including $800 million in March alone, with the result that government cash is now only 4 per cent of government yearly spending, which I think the minister will admit is one of the lowest levels in history, would he indicate to the House if this is the result of government fiscal planning, or has the redemption of Canada Savings Bonds and the Canadian dollar exchange drain taken the government really off guard?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCTION IN GOVERNMENT CASH BALANCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question is highly argumentative, but I will say this in answer to it. The government consciously drew down its cash balance last year as part of its debt management policy. This had the effect for most of the year, in fact most of 1973, of relieving pressure on interest rates and keeping them lower than they otherwise would have been.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCTION IN GOVERNMENT CASH BALANCES

subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCTION IN GOVERNMENT CASH BALANCES

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) is having serious difficulty being heard. Perhaps we could have a little co-operation from hon. members.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
There are no standards, no criteria or no guidelines in the legislation. The discretion in the cabinet is completely unfettered. Yesterday the minister tried to provide some sort of explanation. I quote from his explanation which is recorded at page 1938 of Hansard:
Customary profit margin could be defined differently for each level of distribution. For example, the method to be applied could be different for a manufacturer as opposed to the retailer of a product.

For example, the method to be applied could be different for a manufacturer as opposed to a retailer of a product. The term "customary" could be prescribed to the margin realised during a given past period of time.
He then went on to say:
In setting out the manner of determination of customary profit margin, consideration would be given to the prevailing economic climate and the business cycle of the particular sector. In addition, the guidelines would be sufficiently flexible to take into account their application to firms operating at low levels of profit or at a loss, or to new businesses.
Again, this does not tell us what guidelines the cabinet will follow. It is an example of arbitrary discretionary power.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: How would you define them?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
It does not tell us what research work the cabinet will take into account when setting these guidelines or what opportunity will be provided for those affected, such as manufacturers and distributors, to make their views known to the government when a proposed profit margin is to be put in place. Will they be given an opportunity to be heard? None of this is provided for in the legislation and no guarantee was contained in the undertaking given by the minister yesterday. More important still, there is no procedure for reviewing a cabinet decision. It is an arbitrary determination by cabinet, that is all.
I would ask hon. members to consider the powers proposed to be given to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. Section 56(1) (b) gives the Commission power to impose what is, in effect, an excess profits tax. This is no ordinary tax. It is a tax imposed in an arbitrary and possibly discriminatory manner, and, as was pointed out yesterday, by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), it is a tax introduced without reference to a ways and means motion. It is a tax of a nature which provides revenue to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and, as such, it should have been introduced in the course of a budget.
The bill also gives the Restrictive Trades Practices Commission power to accept a report of any government-appointed body or person relating to price increases. It gives the Commission power to accept the results of research and investigation and inquiries leading to related reports. All this information is admissible in evidence before the Commission. Again, no person affected or likely to be affected by an order of the Commission has the right of cross-examination, the right of access to the persons who prepared any of these reports or conducted any of these investigations. There is no right to challenge the validity of any of the information which is placed before the Commission. This is a further example of arbitrary power conferred, in this instance, on a Commission. It is a power which I, for one, will oppose.
But the most arbitrary power of all is the discretionary power of the cabinet under section 58 to vary or rescind any order of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. Moreover, changing an order made by the RTPC involves no right to a hearing, no right of defence, no right of review. All the procedural rights given to the parties before the Commission are over-ridden and usurped when
May 2, 1974

the cabinet steps in to vary or rescind an order. The cabinet has complete discretion in this regard. There are no standards, no criteria, no due process of procedure. It is just gut reaction, and that is exactly what the bill involves.
Our concern in attacking the bill from this side of the House is not founded in any way on a desire to condone profiteering or gouging by big business. The point is that the bill does not do the job. As the leader of the New Democratic Party correctly stated, its proclamation will do absolutely nothing to stop inflation. More important, it may lull Canadians into a false sense of complacency; it may lull them into thinking something is being done about inflation when in fact nothing will be done. To the extent that the government proposes to apply this bill to certain industries or articles, or classes of articles, it would represent an unprecedented exercise of arbitrary executive power, uneven, inequitable, and, in some cases, counter-productive.
I should like to repeat what was said by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) after the conclusion of the last session of parliament, on January 17:
My concern and the concern of the Progressive Conservative Party is not for the big interests and the highly organized groups which have enough muscle and financial reserve to remain comfortable through periods of escalating inflation-those which can stabilize their own situation sufficiently to ride high and relatively unscathed through endless boom-bust cycles.
Our concern is for the unorganized worker who sustains terrible losses in real income in today's circumstances and who always faces the threat of unemployment as the cycle moves on. Our concern is for the small Canadian business and for the diligent Canadian salary-earner who has struggled to put a modest amount into savings for his family's future needs and for his own retirement.
That is the concern of the Progressive Conservative Party and the bill before us will do nothing to meet that concern.
In summary, the bill reflects a government without leadership, a government which lacks a firm hand at the tiller. The performance yesterday of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) prompted an exodus of other ministers from the chamber reminiscent of rats deserting a sinking ship. It is bad enough that the bill was not presented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), as it should have been had the government been really serious about it. But for the minister to be left alone in the House at the peak of his presentation yesterday was the ultimate insult; it supposes the virtual collapse of the government. The bill was hastily conceived and thrown together as a sop to the NDP. It was not carefully thought out either as to substance or as to procedure. It gave no evidence of leadership or firm direction on economic questions and the statements of the minister and of the Prime Minister subsequent to its introduction have done nothing to correct that failing. But most important, it will do nothing to tackle the real problems of inflation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate for two reasons; first, to reply to some of the rather hasty criticisms which have been made by spokesmen for the opposition, and, second, to expand upon the remarks made by my colleague the Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Profiteering Practices
Affairs (Mr. Gray) as to the purpose of the bill and the intentions of the government with respect to its application.
Let me begin by saying this categorically: the Government of Canada is determined to deal with profiteering and gouging.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: If parties opposite wish to take a contrary position, which means taking a stand in opposition to this bill, that is their business. To say the bill is inadequate or imperfect is one thing; there is always the possibility for improvements to be made in committee. But when the opposition simply opposes the bill, I suggest their attitude is hypocritical.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I interpret that opposition as being political manoeuvring which indicates there is no serious concern for the problems of profiteering and gouging that is basically the reason that this government has introduced this bill. The government has only one purpose in this bill, and that purpose is to deal with profiteering and gouging, nothing else. It is not meant to be a substitute for over-all price and wage control. It is not meant to be a substitute for selective price and wage control, or selective price control as advocated by the NDP. We have taken a position that is in opposition to the application of over-all wage and price control under present circumstances. We are still of that view, though I am not quite sure whether the party opposite is. During this debate I would certainly welcome a clarification of the position of the Progressive Conservative party on the problem of controlling inflation.
One of the reasons I take this position, Mr. Speaker, is this. Yesterday I listened to the reaction to the announcement made by my colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) of an increase in salary for public servants to reflect, and to adjust their salaries to, the recent unprecedented inflation. What was the attitude of the spokesman of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), when this position was placed before the House by the President of the Treasury Board? He said it was inadequate. This, Mr. Speaker, is the party that is in favour of wage controls.
Does this mean that the Progressive Conservative party is in favour of wage controls for the private sector but not for the public service? Is that what is meant by his statement? Certainly, that is the implication of the position taken by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. I suggest this shows that the party opposite, which has pretensions to power, has no policies and does not intend to enunciate any, and hopes that it will drift into office. I doubt whether that attitude is going to appeal to the people of Canada who want action.
I should like to have the positions taken by the various parties clearly defined. Would the Progressive Conservative party let us know now whether they are still in favour of over-all price controls, whether they would still freeze

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
prices for 90 days, or 120 days, whatever period it is; and since they have had a couple of years to think about this idea, would they let us know what is going to happen after the 90 or 120 day period? It seems to me that a party which is criticizing the government for bringing in a bill to deal with profiteering and gouging, not with price control, should define its own position in relation to these central questions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Let us hear from the Minister of Finance on this subject.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: You will on Monday.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Bill C-29 before us is a complicated bill because it is dealing with a complicated question. But may I say this in reply to some of the criticisms that have been made. The bill was not hastily drafted; it was not hastily considered. It has been under consideration for many weeks and months now. I can assure the House that it has been under consideration, not in response to suggestions that have been put forward in the House particularly, but ever since the government announced through the Speech from the Throne that legislation of this kind would be brought forward. This bill is in direct line with the Speech from the Throne and the policies enunciated at that time.
Although this bill was considered over a long period of time, Mr. Speaker, 1 am not suggesting that it cannot be improved. I have had long enough experience in this House and in the business of government to know that all legislation can be improved. Not only that, but I have great respect for my hon. friends opposite. I am sure they can offer some very interesting and constructive suggestions, whether they are members of the Progressive Conservative party, the New Democratic Party or the Credi-tiste party.
I should like to deal generally with the procedure that is contemplated in the bill because it seems to me there has been a good deal of confusion which has been compounded by some of the hasty criticisms made by hon. members opposite. Let me refer to the Food Prices Review Board, which is now in place and established. That board has been monitoring food prices now over a considerable period of time and has operated by persuasion. It has had a considerable number of successes and it has also had a large number of critics. But there is one point upon which all parties are now agreed, and that is that the time has come to put some teeth into the recommendations of the Food Prices Review Board. That is what this bill will do. This bill will establish the enforcement machinery.
On paper, the procedure that is outlined in the bill may appear rather cumbersome.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: That is the understatement of the year.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
However, I regret to say that opposition spokesmen, either deliberately or otherwise, have made it appear much more cumbersome than it actually is. The reason for the procedure in the bill is that the government is concerned to be both fair and effective at one and the same time. I make no apology for an attempt to be fair. I do not want this piece of legislation-and I know the government does not either-to be categorized as a witch hunt. That is not its purpose. We have no intention of

penalizing the manufacturer or the merchant who is making an honest living and taking a normal profit. Indeed, we on the government side want to encourage business of this kind and will take all measures that are reasonable to encourage businessmen who are honest, who are not profiteering or gouging. Our target in this bill is the manufacturer or merchant who is profiteering and gouging. That is the purpose of this bill and is why I said at the beginning that those who are opposed to the bill are opposed to the attack on profiteering and gouging.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: The second point that I should like to make is that, contrary to the assertions that have been made in this House, the government can act quickly on a report of the Food Prices Review Board recommending action. A price stop can be put into effect immediately without any cumbersome machinery. The opposition has misrepresented the bill in this respect, either deliberately or, perhaps, inadvertently. I am not going to attribute motives here but I can assure the members of the House that the bill is quite clear on this point. A price freeze comes into effect at the time of the declaration if we so wish. There is no cumbersome machinery to be dealt with. There is, however, machinery to protect

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister whether he would be good enough to read the clause in the bill that provides what he says is provided-that is to say, that without any further hearing a declaration is made and the price is frozen. Would he please read the clause in the bill that makes that provision?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I have read it, Mr. Speaker. It would not be appropriate for me, on second reading of the bill, to read clauses of the bill, but I can assure the hon. gentlemen that there is provision for this procedure. As soon as a declaration is made, a price freeze can come into effect, and no one can raise prices for 30 days without notice. This effectively freezes prices for 30 days.
It is also important-and this is why I emphasize the point of fairness-that Canadian businessmen should be enabled to raise their prices if this is warranted by cost increases, and normal mark-ups and profits should be permitted. To act otherwise would be grossly discriminatory. And not only that; it would, of course, act in opposition to what I am sure every member of this House wants, and that is to encourage honest businessmen to produce as much as possible. That is our purpose, and I am sure it is the purpose of everyone in this House. So, we have to establish procedures to ensure that the action we take is fair and legitimate, and that all the merchants concerned have an opportunity of appealing if they disagree with the judgment of the officials.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that food products are not our only concern. There are other products in respect of which the government believes action may be required and where action will be taken. May I deal briefly with the suggestion made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), not only on this occasion but on other occasions. I

think it is part of the official platform of that party, this idea of a general prices review board.
It was suggested that this is an alternative the government could have employed instead of using the procedures established in this bill, that is the government might have appointed a general prices review board. We looked very carefully at that alternative and we came to the conclusion that this would have produced unnecessary bureaucracy. Moreover, it was suggested that we could have included a number of other things including services. It seems to us that the reaction to such a proposal would justifiably have been that this is political window dressing. That is the charge that has been made against this bill. I can assure the House that if the government had brought in a general prices review board which purported to have all these powers which were directed at only the question of profiteering and gouging it would have appeared as an inflated proposal that should be condemned out of hand as unnecessary bureaucracy, and that is why we proceeded as we did.
The basic assumption underlying this bill, and I believe it is a justifiable assumption, is that profiteering and gouging are the exception and not the rule in Canada. It is also assumed that the particular circumstances which have led to recent rapid increases, and that facilitate profiteering and gouging, are of a temporary nature, and, although they will persist for some time, we believe they are not of an indefinite duration. The government therefore decided to monitor pricing practices in areas other than food products by a selective approach, by instituting inquiries in important areas where profiteering and gouging could have widespread and pervasive effects, but also, and this is an important provision of the bill, retain freedom of action to act even without an inquiry.
So this machinery which has been described as cumbersome could in fact be put into effect quickly, and could be very effective in dealing with the only problem with which this bill is concerned, namely that of profiteering and gouging.

I submit that while the action that we are taking looks less impressive than the establishment of a general prices review board, in fact it is likely to be more effective. It is likely to be more effective because it will be a good deal less wasteful and less bureaucratic for the intended purpose.
Now, I come to the question of services. This is another major question raised by spokesmen for the opposition. I would like to deal briefly with it as I would like the opposition to know that we did very seriously consider whether or not we should include services within the scope of the legislation. They were omitted for three reasons. In saying that, I would like to make it clear that if a case can be made for putting some of these services back in the bill, because there are serious omissions, the government would not be strongly opposed. Indeed, we would look sympathetically at any suggestion that would be made in this field, if it were constructive. Let me explain why at the initial stages we took services out.
If you look first at services like hairdressing, laundries and things of this kind, the government was very doubtful whether one would want to proffer charges of profiteering and gouging in service industries of this kind. Then we come to the major service industries in the financial field, like banking, money lending and other financial institutions. The problem here is that they do not lend themselves to the kind of procedures provided in this bill. Moreover, many of them are under the supervision of government agencies and to add them to this bill might create some confusion, and probably would not add to the effectiveness of what is being done now.
The third class, of course, includes services such as transportation, telephone rates. These kind of services are now under public control and certainly there would be no point in putting them under this bill. As I say, these are the reasons we left services out, and if the House or parliament decides in its wisdom that services should be included, the government is not particularly opposed. What we did not want to do was mislead the people. We want this bill to be effective, and the place where it can be most effective is in the field of goods.
We now come to the question of land. Everyone will agree that probably the greatest inflation we have seen in this country is in respect of the price of land. Again, when we looked at the machinery for controlling the price of land we doubted whether the kind of machinery in this bill which is to deal with profiteering and gouging could be applied in any very simple way, at least in respect of the transactions by individuals in land. Moreover, we know from our own experience, and all of us know this, that the provinces in many ways are in a better position to deal with questions of land prices than is the federal

Profiteering Practices
government. As I say, we are not opposed to taking action against or in respect of land prices, but we are a little doubtful whether this is the place that action could be most effective. The main element of increased prices of housing is the increased cost of land. We can take action where the price of building supplies and materials are concerned as that does lie within the ambit of this bill. Therefore, housing is included. The price of land does involve a difficult problem.
In brief, this bill, although far-reaching, and one of the most far-reaching pieces of legislation brought before this House in recent years, is nevertheless limited. It is specifically limited in its approach not because the government is timid, and not because it is lacking in seriousness, but because it wants to concentrate its efforts where practical results have some chance of being achieved. That is the purpose and the philosophy of the bill. That is why I reject the charge of the hon. member for York South that this bill is a piece of political window dressing. It is put forward, I can assure the House, after mature consideration of the alternatives. All the alternatives that have been put forward by the opposition were considered by the government before this particular approach was decided upon. These alternatives were rejected not because the government lacked courage but because, to use the hon. member's own words, we thought it might look like window dressing.
Now, on a subject like profiteering and gouging it is easy to be demagogic. I do not know of any subject on which it is easier to make a rousing speech, but it is not so easy to devise fair and effective measures to cope with unwarranted price increases in a free and open society. This bill may be imperfect but I can assure the House that such imperfections as it may have are not deliberate. It may be perhaps that we have not been able to foresee every issue and circumstance, but I can assure the House that the government intends to use the machinery to do everything reasonable to curb profiteers and gougers starting from the day the bill becomes law.
In this connection I was somewhat taken back looking back at the speech made by the hon. member for York South when he was dealing with this issue. He said he is not opposed to the principle of this bill. He said he is opposed to profiteering and gouging but that he does not think the government is serious about it. He quoted the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as recorded at page 1943 of Hansard:
I turn, therefore, to a report in the Montreal Star of April 25, a report which appeared in a number of other papers. Here is part of this report. I quote:
The Prime Minister indicated that the legislation might not be
proclaimed until needed. He suggested that the threat of it would be
enough to stop companies from profiteering.

I read from Hansard

of March 13, 1974 at page 473 where the Prime Minister is recorded as saying:
When gouging or profiteering has been established before the independent board and those who are alleged to have gouged have been given a chance to state their case, if they do not take corrective action that is when we will act and not on some arbitrary suggestion by the hon. member.
That is the attitude of the government. We would not have brought this legislation forward if we did not intend to use it. Why would we have gone to all that trouble?

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) who has just spoken on this bill has made a useful contribution in that while he may not have told us what the bill will do he certainly clarified what it will not do. He has told us that it is not going to resolve the problem of inflation, that it is not going to provide selective price controls, and that it is solely aimed at stopping undue profiteering, despite the fact that he then went on to say that profiteering in Canada was the exception rather than the rule, and that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) has already said that there is no evidence of widespread abuse in the country.
So here is a minister seeking to defend a bill, and doing it very poorly, who has only succeeded in telling us that the bill will not do most of the things that the government has been trying to persuade the public it will do, namely, help in the matter of inflation and provide some protection with respect to price controls.
The minister says that the government has introduced this legislation in order to stop some forms of profiteering. He has made a very poor case to prove that. He says that upon a declaration prices will be frozen. I ask him to find where there is any such provision in clauses 51 and 52? Prices cannot be frozen without a reference to the courts. The minister should know that, if he has read this legislation. I suspect he has not studied it very closely.
He has been dragged in to defend this legislation because the two ministers who are the arch apostles of high profits would cut very inconspicuous figures in this debate trying to prove that we should stop profiteering, profiteering which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs says does not exist, and which the Secretary of State for External Affairs says is the exception rather than the rule.
I think we ought to take a look at this bill, which is supposed to deal with profiteering practices, in the light of the total picture which faces the country with respect to inflation. I think every member will recognize that the rapidly escalating cost of living is one of the two major problems disturbing the Canadian people. The other, of course, is unemployment.
The problem of rising living costs has aroused the Canadian people as nothing else I have seen in many years. When you have an increase in a living cost of 10.4 per cent, an increase in the price of food of 18.6 per cent, and when you have the cost of living for hundreds of thousands of workers rising faster than their real income then you have a crisis which is stirring this nation as nothing else has done for many years.
Since the beginning of this parliament the members of the New Democratic Party have taken a very realistic approach to this problem. We have recognized that inflation is part of a worldwide trend, and that there are
May 2, 1974

factors which are beyond the control of any national government. We have said repeatedly that just a freeze on prices and wages is unrealistic and could be very unjust, that there is no way in which the government of Canada can fix the price of imported products-citrus fruits, coffee, tea, cocoa, bauxite, natural rubber, and certain sophisticated machinery which we must buy outside this country. The prices of those commodities are set by the countries that produce them, and we must pay those prices or do without those commodities. There is no way that we can freeze those prices.
We also recognize that merely to freeze wages and prices is to lock in a great many injustices on the one hand, and a great deal of excess profiteering on the other. The report of the Senate Committee showed that there are 500,000 families in Canada, called by that committee the working poor, whose incomes are lower than if they were on welfare. To freeze their incomes is to freeze them into unconscionable poverty. And at the same time to freeze the profits of the banks and the oil companies is to put them in paradise. Therefore, we have suggested a two-pronged attack on this whole question of the rising cost of living.
Since the beginning of this parliament we have first of all suggested that parliament and the government must make provision to help those who are most vulnerable to the rising cost of living. The government has responded to some extent. There were increases in old age pensions. The old age pension was put on the basis of the rising cost of living rather than being limited to a 2 per cent increase. There was an increase in veterans' pensions. Last year there was some reduction in personal income tax for those in the lower and middle income groups. Increased family allowances are another example. These things have helped, but I want to point out that the rising cost of living in the meantime has eaten up all the gains that these people have made.
We pressed for other things. We suggested that commodities which are essential for every family, and particularly for those on lower incomes, ought to have assistance by way of subsidies or by way of reduced sales taxes. Some of this has been done. The government did introduce subsidies on milk, beef and bread. Whether they have reached the consumer or not is something we are waiting for the government to discover because it has not yet completed its studies in that regard. And some sales taxes have been reduced on items like children's clothing. We have not reduced such things as the sales tax on building materials. We have not provided any tax credits for people in lower income brackets. But the government did move, and I want to give it credit. It moved, sometimes reluctantly, sometimes on being pushed very hard, and it did take steps to cushion the effect of rising living costs, particularly on those in the lower income brackets.
But when we come to the second prong of the attack which the NDP had been advocating with respect to the rising cost of living, the government has been adamant in its refusal. Broadly speaking, we suggested four things. First of all, we suggested the setting up of a prices review board to monitor prices, with power to freeze prices where increases were unjustified, with power to roll back prices, and to move into certain areas and hold prices at a level that would be fair and just.
Profiteering Practices
We have said that along with this it would be necessary to establish a two-price system for a great many commodities. If this government merely fixes the price of a commodity and that price is less than the one producers can get on the world market, that commodity will go out of the country. Therefore, we require a two-price system, with export controls and, in some cases, an export tax. There is little value in fixing a price if the commodity is not available. Many commodities are made in this country which bring in substantial profits if they are sold on the world market. I do not see why Canadians should be required to pay high prices for steel, lumber, cement or anything else produced in this country merely because corporations can obtain a higher return if they ship such commodities out of the country. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), when answering the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), has completely rejected a two-price system for selected areas which should be brought under control.
The third thing we have suggested is the reduction of mortgage interest rates to 6 per cent; and the fourth thing, an excess profits tax to siphon off some surplus profits being made at present.
The government should realize that the people who work with hand and brain in this country to produce its wealth, and whose real income in the last quarter of 1973, compared with the last quarter of 1972, was down by $5.50 per week, will not tolerate that situation. When the working people note the distribution of our gross national product and see that the share for corporate profits has gone up and the share for wages and salaries has gone down, they will not accept it. That kind of redistribution of income in reverse will not be condoned or accepted by the Canadian people.
Although the government has moved on the first prong of our attack and cushioned some of the effects of rising costs of living on those who are most drastically affected, it has consistently refused to intervene in the economy, something it must do if the ordinary people of this country are to be protected against profiteering and against the high prices corporations can charge and demand if they threaten to ship their products out of this country.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs who spoke this afternoon said, in response to my leader, that he was sure the NDP is not for sale, that the government did not throw sops to the NDP or anyone else and had acted according to its conscience. His conscience must be guilty.

The government could respond to the first of the two prongs of the NDP program and raise old age

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
pensions and other allowances without arousing criticism, but it is not prepared to challenge the corporate structure of this country.
The member who preceded me wondered why the Secretary of State for External Affairs had spoken in this debate, since its subject matter is not within his purview. I suggest he entered the debate to assure the Bay Street barons that they need not worry about this bill because, after all, profiteering is the exception in this country, not the rule. The government's attitude with respect to intervening in the economy to provide equity and economic justice has become increasingly apparent in recent months.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), addressing a joint meeting of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Manitoba and the Law Society of Manitoba at Winnipeg, on April 19, 1974, said in part:
One of the red herrings injected into this debate, particularly by the NDP, is that the corporate profits of Canada's manufacturers and processors are now so high that the reduction in their tax burden is completely unjustified.
Certainly there has been a substantial improvement in business earnings, an improvement in which Canada's manufacturers and processors have fully shared. Certainly there is some point of proper balance to be struck. But profits cannot be considered in a vacuum. They must be considered in relation to our urgent requirement for sharply increased capital investment...
It must be obvious to nearly everyone other than Mr. Lewis and followers that the money to finance this huge increase in capital investment by Canadian manufacturers must come from somewhere.
It is apparent that the money is to come from the consumers of this country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: From ordinary taxpayers.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes, from the taxpayers of this country who have had to pick up the burden of the corporate tax concessions which this government provided last year, with the help of the Progressive Conservative party.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) sings a similar song. Speaking to the conference board in Canada in Winnipeg on April 3, he said in part:
Of course, the problem, according to the New Democratic Party, is profits. The NDP believes profits aren't really necessary. This government knows profits are necessary to continued industrial growth- provided that a significant share of these profits is pumped back into expansion and employment.
Later in that speech he said:
Putting it another way, the proportion of earnings retained for corporate purposes was at an all-time high. Our manufacturers are using their profits to finance expansion-and that's what we want.
That is the government's position. I can understand why neither of those ministers wants to defend this bill. How can they talk about wanting to stop profiteering when they tell everybody that profiteering is marvellous, that the more profits you make the more jobs you create. It is dangerous to suggest the thesis that the consumer of this country, when he purchases an article, should provide for its cost of production, for the servicing and retirement of capital debt and for a reasonable return to shareholders, and, in addition, enough money to enable the corporation to retain sufficient earnings for future capital expansion. When a man buys a pair of shoes, he can legitimately be expected to pay for overhead and return to the entre-

preneur on capital investment. Should he also be required to pay, in addition, for the construction of a new plant or the expansion of an existing plant. That is the thesis the government is advancing.
Now, let us look at another aspect of the government's approach to intervention in the economy. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) made reference to the fact that the Food Prices Review Board was set up. He said this act will now put teeth in the Food Prices Review Board. I ask him what prevented them from putting teeth in that board when it was established.
As a matter of fact, when this matter was before the committee on food prices, representatives of the New Democratic Party moved that the Food Prices Review Board be given the necessary power to freeze and roll back prices where it was found necessary to do so. That amendment was defeated by both Liberal and Conservative members.
When the matter was before the House, the members of this party pleaded with the government to put some teeth in the Food Prices Review Board. The government refused. Why did they refuse? If they now believe the Food Prices Review Board should have teeth, why did they not give it teeth a year ago? The fact is they had no intention of the Food Prices Review Board having teeth. The Food Prices Review Board was set up because there was public clamour for the government to do something. That piece of deception not having worked, they are trying a second piece of deception, that is giving the Food Prices Review Board rubber teeth.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
The government is not going to fool anybody by the kind of statements that were made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The fact is that this piece of legislation is a last act of desperation. This bill is an attempt to perpetrate a cruel hoax on the people of Canada by seeking to convince them that the government intends to do something when it is increasingly apparent they do not intend to do anything about the large scale profiteering that is going on by the corporations of this country. If the government wanted to deal with profiteering, why has it taken so long?
It is very interesting that when we argued about putting teeth in the Food Prices Review Board, it was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) who said the government did not have the constitutional authority. That is what he said a year ago. He now finds it has constitutional authority.
I was tremendously impressed by the answer which the minister gave when questioned by the press on this matter. They asked how come he said they did not have constitutional authority a year ago and now he brings in a bill that he claims gives them constitutional authority to do something about profiteering. The minister's answer should be put on the record because it is one of the great and immortal sayings of all times. This is his answer:
It doesn't appear to me now the way it appeared to appear to me then.

Today the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the House-it cannot be denied because it is on the record-that profiteering in this country is the exception rather than the rule. Therefore, we are going to have legislation to deal with profiteering that is not widespread and profiteering which is the exception rather than the rule.

And temporary. As a matter of fact, I wonder where these people have been. Look at the oil industry profits for the first three months of this year. Imperial Oil had profits of over $1 million a day for the first quarter with $4 a barrel oil. Imagine what their profits will be with $6.50 a barrel oil.
The minister says that profiteering is the exception rather than the rule. This country today is riddled with profiteering. As the hon. member for York South pointed out yesterday, in the first three months of this year, 111 companies in Canada showed profit increases of 70 per cent over last year. Is that not excessive profiteering? Apparently the Secretary of State for External Affairs does not consider that profiteering.
The fact is this government considers profits to be a good thing. Both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have said that profiteering helps to create jobs and therefore it is a good thing. Then why this bill? We have this bill because the government knows the public are fed up with seeing the workers' share of the gross national product going down and corporate profits going up. This government knows it has to do something. It is doing something by perpetrating a farce. I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we in this party will not be accomplices to a farce of this kind.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION

This legislation is brought in after one year during which the government has consistently refused to do anything about these excess profits. It is

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
brought in now because the government faces the prospect of going to the country. I have never had much faith in a deathbed repentance and I do not think the electorate will have any faith in a deathbed repentance, either. We in this party do not believe this bill was ever seriously intended as a measure to stop gouging and profiteering. We think that in the main it was an attempt to convince the public that the government was keeping a commitment made by the Prime Minister on February 28 when he said his administration would not allow gouging and profiteering through windfall profits at the expense of the Canadian people.
Yesterday, the leader of our party dealt with his act very effectively. Let me just reiterate three points which I believe ought to be reinforced in view of the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-they relate to three of the basic weaknesses of the bill. First, it can be put on the statute books without becoming effective in any way, shape or form until a declaration is made by the cabinet. It could sit on the statute books as a monument to the government's good intentions, and nothing more. It could, of course, as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has suggested, be a deterrent. I notice he said this outside the House, but so that he will not deny it, let me quote what he said inside the House as reported in Hansard at page 1940:
In any event, the existence of this legislation should act as a deterrent to those who might otherwise feel they can engage in profiteering with impugnity.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I can understand the minister's concern. He produces a piece of legislation, then he goes outside the House and says he will only use it sparingly and that it will only be called upon to deal with serious and obvious cases of profiteering. When he had damned his own legislation with faint praise I can understand his concern when it is brought to the attention of the House of Commons and the people of Canada. I think the Canadian people will be quick to realise that this legislation is a sham, a snare and a delusion.
The second obvious weakness is that there is no provision for any monitoring agency in this process, though we have talked over the years about a Prices Review Board, about a continuing and on-going process of canvassing prices; about a board with power to impose selective controls, freeze prices and roll back prices. There is no such power here. This legislation covers only a limited field. The Secretary of State was really talking with his tongue in his cheek when he said the reason the legislation did not cover services was that the government did not wish to deal with hairdressers, barbers, people in the service industries. He knows this is not mandatory legislation but permissive legislation and that if the bill covers services, as it should because services represent about 25 per cent of the Canadian economy, the government could be selective. Nobody expects the government to interfere with hairdressing, for example. But it could interfere with interest rates; it could interfere with the profits made by the land developers; it could interfere with what is going on in connection with house-building programs. The reason services are left out is that the government does not want to tackle this important field.
My final point is this. The nub of this legislation lies in the fact that when the minister talks about ability to freeze prices or roll back prices-and I deny he possesses that power, except through the courts-he fails to tell us at what level prices should be frozen, or to what level prices should be rolled back. The words in the act are "to a customary margin of profit". And what is that? The bill does not say. It does not specify a certain return on capital investment. It does not specify a certain return related to the percentage of sales. Not at all, Mr. Speaker. When the minister himself put out the explanatory information for the edification of the public, the information talks of levels of profit for the previous year.

I say again that it would take a very long time to explain the technicalities of the bill, and that this can be done in committee. But personally, I am satisfied, and I think all of my colleagues in government are satisfied, that that provision is in the bill. If there is any ambiguity in the bill, then we are prepared to remove it.
The other point that I want to make has to do with the first 10 or 15 minutes of the hon. gentleman's speech of about 45 minutes. During that time there was a period when I was almost prepared to concede that he thought we were doing some of the right things over here; and indeed he said so. But what was brought out in that period, which again tends to annoy me I must confess, was not a question relating to profiteering alone. Going back to my quotations from Hansard, all that was really talked about was profiteering and a means of getting rid of what is known as gouging. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands opened up the whole question of high profits, big business and uneven distribution. God knows, coming from the province of Newfoundland I am as aware of that as he is, and I say again, nobody in this House is more concerned to see that there is a decent distribution of wealth and that these people at the lower end of the scale get a decent break. I am glad to see finally that they are getting it.
Let me go on to make one point clear, with which I think hon. gentlemen will be in agreement. Newfoundland for the first time, indeed all of Atlantic Canada, specifically the fish plant workers and the fishermen, are getting a decent wage for their work and decent prices. I see that as being just one of the finest breakthroughs we have had in a long time. I am surprised by the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) that we ought to have wage controls in a province like Newfoundland or

on the east coast. I thoroughly agree with what another hon. member has said in this regard, that this would be a disaster for the poor people of this country, and I reject that out of hand.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that my time may be limited somewhat as a result of the private members' hour, but I do want to say this. He himself said yesterday that they had important amendments they believe they could make to the bill if it went into the committee. Other people over there have said that they are looking for clarification in respect of the bill, yet on both sides we hear hon. members saying that they do not want to even look at it in the committee. They want to throw it out before it gets there. That to me is a completely irrational attitude which means only one thing so far as I am concerned. It is pretty hard to believe that this party is genuinely concerned about gouging and profiteering- pretty darn hard to believe it-if they will not take this bill and bring it together in a co-operative way in the committee in order to see what can be done with it.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I repeat that it is a much stronger bill than the NDP party in particular has talked about. With his particular kind of rhetoric, and I admire it, of course, the leader of the NDP yesterday talked about the so-called elongated process. Well, it may not be an elongated process, but in his mouth it was a distorted process. What he said was that so many steps had to be taken before a price freeze could come in that it would literally take the skin off the Canadian consumer, and I remember that phrase. He is wrong about that; he is completely wrong. The freeze can be put on, and I hope that if I do not have the opportunity other speakers will go into this in more detail. It is misleading of our position and it is misleading of this bill.
Let me now deal rather quickly with the three points made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. He talked about the ineffectiveness of this measure. What he really said was that this is some kind of smokescreen we are putting up. I say to you, that is not so. I say to you that if this House passes this bill I am satisfied this government will act and act at once.

speechtext: What about the prices review board?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
My hon. friend uses the prices review board to his advantage when he wants to dismiss it, yet we hear 50 questions asking about what we are going to do, and in some respects praising the prices review board. This is such a double standard I have never seen anything like it for years. I can agree again with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands as I have very little confidence in the business community being threatened by a big stick. I perfectly agree with him that the wagging of a finger is not likely to have much effect.
May 2, 1974

I repeat that it is our intention, and it will be our intention when this legislation passes, to move and to move decisively. Once this order is issued this price freeze becomes effective. Furthermore, there is the mechanism here for rolling back those prices. I am talking about gouging and the things which the NDP party in particular has emphasized for so long. I am not talking about the whole range of what my friend might regard as inequities in the economic system. There are other measures and other methods of dealing with those. He touched upon some of them when he talked about our bolstering incomes at the lower levels of our society.
I do not question the suggestion that there should be ways for us to get after some of these corporations. Does my friend think that I and a great many of my colleagues here are immune to some of these kinds of things or are unaware of them? That is nonsense. Just put this bill in operation and I will assure you that you will see things move very quickly.
The hon. member talks about continuity once again. I am not sure what he means by continuity, but I do know that mechanisms in the bill provide for an ongoing organization as he will see if he studies the bill objectively. The hon. member's leader yesterday said something about a part-time board, or something of that sort. That is just not the case. It is part of the organization but it will be full-time in the sense of its own activity.
If the hon. member means by continuity a continuing review of prices, we do have a prices review board and other mechanisms through which to do that. The hon. member talks about the complexity of this bill, as have others, and of putting into the piece of legislation one guide as to what constitutes an appropriate level of profit, or whatever one wishes to call it. That is, of course, the height of impossibility. It just cannot be done. Surely, one has to look at each industry, one after the other, in order to determine what represents an appropriate level of profit. For some industries it may very well be a reflection of the investment on earnings, or whatever the case might be, but to suggest that a bill can in fact spell out just how profiteering or gouging shall be measured in all industries, and perhaps do it in one or two sentences, is unrealistic. That merely reflects the total unreality of the arguments that have been coming from the opposition with regard to this measure.
I repeat that hon. members of the opposition said at the initial stages, and I think one or two of their members have said it recently, that our actions in this regard are a hoax. I reject that, and I say that to prove this is not a hoax, let us give second reading to this bill and get it to the committee where perhaps we can bring about the improvements that hon. members would want to see.
