subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPIES OF CONTRACTS BETWEEN VANCOUVER HARBOURS BOARD AND CERTAIN FIRMS RESPECTING USE OF PIERS IN 1973 AND 1974
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of all contracts between the National Harbours Board in Vancouver and the following firms (a) Empire Stevedoring Co. Ltd. (b) Canadian Stevedoring Co. Ltd. (c) Canadian National Railways respecting the use of Ballantyne Pier, Lapointe Pier and Centennial Pier for the years 1973 and 1974.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out at the beginning of my remarks that I placed Motion No. 10 on the order paper because I am concerned about the future development of the port of Vancouver and also about the manner in which Mr. William Rathie, the local member of the National Harbours Board and Chairman of the Vancouver Port Authority, is acting in administering that port and its facilities. I might also point out, Mr. Speaker, that I asked to have this matter posted for debate because I am not in the least satisfied with the answer I received from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay).
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) stated:
Mr. Speaker, the documents requested are private and confidential. They are contracts for operating certain shipping terminals in the port of Vancouver which actively compete for business with the port of Seattle, and making them open for public inspection could prejudice their position. I would therefore ask the hon. member to withdraw his motion.
27451-62,1

May 2, 1974
Vancouver National Harbours Board
Mr. Speaker, it is beyond my understanding why the parliamentary secretary could come to the conclusion that these contracts are of a confidential nature as they have, to the best of my knowledge, been signed between the National Harbours Board and the stevedoring companies. There can be no question that the release of this information can in any way jeopardize the public interest or Vancouver's competitive position with the port of Seattle. You see, Mr. Speaker, the rates charged for stevedoring are already public knowledge and the contracts signed by the NHB and these companies can have no bearing on these rates.
It is my belief that Mr. Rathie made the unilateral decision to have the NHB operate these facilities simply to allow the companies named in the motion to opt out of their responsibilities to pay the general purpose and business taxes to the city of Vancouver. What happened, Mr. Speaker, was that Mr. Rathie arbitrarily and without consultation with the Vancouver city council changed the operating nature of these facilities by cancelling the contracts in force up to October 31, 1973. This is what Mr. Rathie did on November 19, 1973: He wrote to the Vancouver city assessor stating that the facilities in question, which were under lease from the NHB to these companies, had been cancelled effective November 1, 1973, and further stated that the National Harbours Board was now the owner and occupier of these premises.
In his reply of November 30 to Mr. Rathie, Mayor Art Phillips of the city of Vancouver took the position, with which I fully agree, of supporting the findings of the Vancouver Court of Revision that the companies in question had been properly placed on the city's assessment rolls. The mayor further stated that the current practice could only be regarded as an effort to avoid taxes to the city of Vancouver, as there was no visible change in the use of the properties. I stress that-no visible change in the use of the properties. In his reply of December 10 to the mayor, Mr. Rathie took the position that these changes had taken place on November 1, 1973 and there was nothing further he could do.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the minister the result of this shady deal between Mr. Rathie and these stevedoring companies. The 1973 general purpose tax assessment, a realty tax for all purposes, was deemed to be $518,781, while the business tax in that year was assessed at $98,940, for a grand total of $617,721. From the position the city has taken, the estimated revenue for 1974 is as follows: General purpose taxes would have been $537,536 and the business tax $110,580, for a total revenue of $648,156. Under the existing granting formula for grants in lieu of taxes the city expects to receive in 1974 the paltry sum of $153,536, for a loss of revenue of $494,620, nearly half a million dollars the city is being cheated out of by this bit of chicanery.
As you can realize, this is not an insignificant amount. It is close to one-half million dollars. I would point out that in his address to the Vancouver Merchants' Exchange Limited on February 19 of this year, Mr. Del Taylor, Chairman of the National Harbours Board stated:
... about one-half million dollars goes to the municipalities around the Port of Vancouver for our grants in lieu of taxes to pay for the federal government's share of the services we use...

While Mr. Taylor may be proud of the fact that all the municipalities concerned receive some half a million dollars collectively, I must point out that due to Mr. Rathie's machinations, the city of Vancouver alone stands to lose just about the same amount of money per year. Unless the city fathers can ascertain how much these stevedoring companies, namely Empire Stevedoring, Canadian Stevedoring and the CNR are paying the National Harbours Board per year, they cannot ascertain how big the rip-off is.
Because of the fact that Mr. Rathie is in the position of being a tsar with regard to the port of Vancouver, and because he has consistently acted in that manner ever since his appointment to his present position to the detriment of the port, I am convinced that a totally new structure is needed to administer the affairs of one of the most important ports in Canada. To ensure consultation with the surrounding municipalities and to allow for input from them I would propose the following new administrative structure. I would hope that the parliamentary secretary to the minister would draw this to the attention of the minister in case he does not read this in Hansard. Vancouver should be removed as a designated NHB port and reconstituted under the provision of the 1964 Harbours Commissions Act similar to the Harbour Commission operating in New Westminster, the North Fraser Harbour Commission and the South Fraser Harbour Commission. It should be composed of seven members, four from the federal government to ensure federal government control, with one or more of these from the prairie regions because of their concern for grain movements through the port of Vancouver; one from the south shore municipalities; one from the North shore municipalities and one from the western area transport council.
Under this arrangement the port manager would not report to Mr. Rathie but to the assistant deputy minister of marine administration in Ottawa. I might point out that the two Fraser Harbour Commissions operating in this fashion have shown more than marginal profits in recent years, unlike the deficits continually reported for the port of Vancouver. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been in contact with the Vancouver city council and this proposal has the complete support of Mayor Art Phillips and Alderman Setty Pendakur, who is the chairman of the Vancouver City Waterfront Committee.
There is now information circulating in Vancouver that the National Harbours Board, under Mr. Rathie's guidance, is considering an offer to purchase Empire Stevedoring's operation at terminal pier. Because I know that Mr. Rathie is personally involved in a number of stevedoring businesses, I am concerned with a possible conflict of interest in this matter. I am also concerned that Mr. Rathie is using his authority to assist his friends on the waterfront by eliminating their responsibilities to the city of Vancouver and, therefore, I must insist on the production of the contracts, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPIES OF CONTRACTS BETWEEN VANCOUVER HARBOURS BOARD AND CERTAIN FIRMS RESPECTING USE OF PIERS IN 1973 AND 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not exactly surprised that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) is proposing a motion to the effect of which would be to make public contracts between the National Harbours Board in Vancouver, the Empire Steve-
May 2, 1974

doring Company Limited, the Canadian Stevedoring Company Limited and Canadian National Railways. However, I doubt very much whether my hon. colleague has directed much thought to the long-term repercussions of taking such a step. After all, regardless of other considerations, we must ask ourselves whether in this House we want to open to scrutiny all documents which have been drawn up on the understanding that they would be immune to public disclosure. Does this House want to set a precedent which might undermine the whole system under which so many of our vital Canadian Crown corporations have negotiated their business in the past.
Does my friend not appreciate that by disclosing the nature and content of contracts between the National Harbours Board and other companies this House might find itself in an irreversible and embarrasing situation? I do not want to believe that this House would seriously entertain a motion which in the long term might seriously jeopardize Canada's ability to compete actively with our trading neighbours to the south, and that is very important.
I am aware of the fact that there is a very legitimate reason for us to be concerned about whether a Crown corporation is operating in the public good. I am certainly not suggesting that there should be any suppression of disclosure regarding the conduct and viability of our Crown corporations. Contrary to what the hon. member said a few minutes ago, there is no purpose served in divulging the details of a grievance between the NHB and private companies which would quite seriously compromise the relatively competitive standing of the port of Vancouver with respect to competitors in the United States.
Surely, we do not want to publicize the details of arrangements between the NHB and private companies, arrangements that by their very nature are designed to give the port of Vancouver special privileges to make it an economically prosperous alternative to ports in the United States. There is nothing insidious or underhand in maintaining this kind of privacy with respect to these agreements. There is, however, a great danger that by disclosing the kind of information proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) we will be taking, quite unwittingly, action which could permanently damage our ability to compete on a free and open market.
I know that there are a number of other considerations implicit in the motion before us today. For instance, a number of people have expressed concern regarding the question of the NHB paying grants in lieu of taxes. The matter is long and involved, but the NHB has always taken the position that it would pay grants in lieu of taxes as required, but subject to any right of appeal available to any other taxpayer. In the current situation, the NHB has changed its contractual arrangements with operators of terminals in Vancouver so that only grants in lieu of taxes and not full municipal taxes should be assessed. In fact, the city has been collecting full taxes for three years. A judgment was just handed down recently from a provincially appointed hearing and it was in favour of the NHB.
Vancouver National Harbours Board
The NHB has entered into contracts with Empire Stevedoring Company Limited, Canadian Stevedoring Company Limited and Canadian National Railways. In accordance with these contracts, the three companies will provide, perform and carry out services for the NHB incidental to and arising from the operation by the NHB of its premises and facilities as public terminals for the handling, loading and unloading of cargo. In consideration of the said services, the NHB will pay each contractor an amount directly related to the amount of cargo handled by each contractor.
The NHB is the operator and occupier of each facility with supervisory and accounting staff located on the premises. The maximum charges paid by the shipper or steamship line for the use of an NHB facility are controlled by the board. None of the board's facilities is leased and the maintenance of the same is the responsibility of the NHB. As operator and occupier of its own facilities the NHB expects to pay grants in lieu of taxes to the city of Vancouver with respect to each of the three facilities related to the three contracts.
I do not want to get any further involved in the details surrounding these contracts for reasons that I am sure are obvious to all concerned. Various articles have appeared in the press dealing with the subject of taxes paid to the city of Vancouver by the NHB or by tenants of the board. It is quite apparent that these newspaper articles are confusing to the public and some statements have been made which are incorrect.
I do not think that there can be any question that the arrangement which exists between the city of Vancouver and the NHB is an equitable one which allows the NHB to operate a major port facility while extending annual grants to the city. This arrangement has existed for some time and I cannot understand why the status quo has to be upset by speculation alleging that the NHB is somehow deriving benefits from the city of Vancouver at the expense of the taxpayer. Any honest and realistic assessment of this arrangement would prove the contrary, and the port of Vancouver can hardly De considered a liability in terms of its massive and positive impact on the economy of Vancouver and the country as a whole.
Tonnage handled by the port of Vancouver has increased from 35,300,000 tons in 1971 to 36,700,000 tons in 1972 and to more than 40 million tons in 1973. Vancouver is the second largest port in North America. It is rated by the International Association of Port Authorities which met in Amsterdam in 1972, as being the thirteenth largest port in the world based on 1971 figures as compared with Seattle rates as number 25. Vancouver does not want to falter in her position as a major port facility. I believe it should be brought to the attention not only of the hon. member but of all hon. members who may not know that so that they can take it into consideration and understand some of the reasons why the answers were given as they were.
Two new major facilities have been constructed in the inner harbour. Vanterm, a 76 acre container facility, will be one of the most modern in the world and will cost some $30 million. In addition, Lynnterm, on the north shore, a general cargo facility with container capabilities, is being built at an estimated cost of $23 million. As an aside, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
May 2, 1974
Vancouver National Harbours Board
Speaker, construction of a modern dock facility has started at Prince Rupert, and it will comprise 43 acres and cost about $23 million.
In the last two years the National Harbours Board has initiated, and has underway $76 million in facilities. In addition, studies regarding development of the second stage at Roberts Bank, at an estimated cost of some $20 million, are well in hand.
The Port of Vancouver must compete with the port of Seattle where port facilities pay no taxes and a 2 mill levy is applied to property in King County to support that port. It must also compete with Harbour Commission ports in British Columbia where no taxes are paid-New Westminster, Nanaimo and Port Alberni. Thus the Port of Vancouver must keep its costs down.
The National Harbours Board does pay taxes to municipal governments. In 1971 as a system NHB paid $7,418,321, and in 1972 paid $6,640,359 in tax grants to Canadian municipalities. Comments relative to the equipping of the port of Vancouver are not well founded. As a container port it has lacked certain facilities, but in fact Vancouver is bigger, is growing faster and is more efficient than Seattle. The two are not truly comparable. Vancouver is a very big export port. Seattle is very largely a container port.
Comments regarding relatively cheap facilities at Seattle are not well founded. The American Mail Line leases a modern container facility in Seattle, but with no rail connection and no de-stuffing facility. It covers about 20 acres, speaking from memory, and the cost is $1 million per year. That is hardly cheap. No doubt other facilities in Seattle are comparable. They are financed by a tax levy on property and by tax exempt municipal bonds.
It is not the policy of the National Harbours Board to safeguard private companies from taxation. It would be most improper for the board to have such a policy. This is the role of the government, not of Crown corporations unless so directed by government, and this board has not been so directed. The city of Vancouver is in favour of port expansion, and has obvious gains to make. To insist on taxation that would force prices up to a level not competitive with already established west coast ports would be self-defeating.
The board is charged with the responsibility of operating the ports under its jurisdiction in the best interests of Canada. It is under many restraints. Many demands are made upon it by many varied interests. In fact each one of its major decisions is subject to review, and is either authorized by order in council or by Treasury Board. For example, it is required to justify investment of taxpayers' dollars in the major facilities under construction as being in the best interests of Canada and of the port of Vancouver.
The whole subject matter of the National Harbours Board and municipal governments with respect to taxation has been a long and complicated problem for both sides. If we are to take economic estimates of the value of port activities to a municipal area as being equal to $20 per ton of cargo handled, the port of Vancouver meant an annual economic benefit to greater Vancouver of some

$840 million in 1973 alone. With co-operation from municipal governments, railways, industry and other levels of government it is suggested that the port of Vancouver will have an impact of at least $1,600,000,000 plus a year by 1980.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention that Canada has played an extremely active and aggressive role in terms of promotion of her ports. It would be a sad day indeed if we were to allow this posture to be compromised by the disclosure of documents and information passing between the National Harbours Board and private companies. I strongly oppose the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver East. It would serve neither the best interests of Vancouver nor those of Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPIES OF CONTRACTS BETWEEN VANCOUVER HARBOURS BOARD AND CERTAIN FIRMS RESPECTING USE OF PIERS IN 1973 AND 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House this afternoon moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) reads as follows:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of all contracts between the National Harbours Board in Vancouver and the following firms (a) Empire Stevedoring Co. Ltd. (b) Canadian Stevedoring Co. Ltd (c) Canadian National Railways respecting the use of Ballantyne Pier, Lapointe Pier and Centennial Pier for thhe years 1973 and 1974.
As I listened to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), it seemed to me that the crunch argument in this whole matter is whether or not these internal agreements will be made public or kept confidential. As I listened to the hon. member, it seemed he was saying that for the sake of the competitive position of the National Harbours Board in Vancouver vis-a-vis Seattle and other Pacific coast ports, the Board wanted to maintain the confidentiality of these documents so as not to reveal input costs. This is a standard business practice. One does one's best not to reveal input costs to a competitor lest he be placed in a position to better them. I have sympathy for the
May 2, 1974

position put forward by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) concerning the confidentiality of agreements between the National Harbours Board and private companies.
I wish to add briefly to the discussion which was well covered by the hon. member. It would be fitting for me to deal with the ports of Canada with particular reference to our western gateway, Vancouver, one of our largest and most important ports. Canadian ports are an integral part of our national transportation system, linking water and land modes of transportation. Therefore, policy direction, planning and co-ordination are essential to ensure effective and efficient utilization of port facilities to the optimum benefit of all Canadians. In a trading nation such as Canada a port system is essential as an intrinsic part of a national transportation system. I think we in Canada can be very proud of the initiatives we have taken to promote a sophisticated ports system.
In this regard, the National Harbours Board has been singularly effective and any attempt to limit or modify the role it plays would surely be regretted at a later stage. Efforts to capture markets and traffic have been rewarded by increased cargo volume, and this trend should not be interrupted by misguided notions that public airing of private agreements is in the interest of Canada's transportation development.
The National Harbours Board has been extremely flexible in its response to changes in world shipping trends, technological development and international trade patterns. It has ensured that Canadian ports have been established and maintained in terms of both national and international interests and in keeping with Canada's constitutional responsibilities for navigation, shipping and national defence. It has planned carefully but boldly to ensure optimization in recovery of investment as well as allocation of resources, thereby providing maximum benefit to the country.
The National Harbours Board has also provided an organizational framework which is responsive to our national political, economic and social needs and is capable of operating within a highly competitive commercial environment. Vancouver is gradually emerging as a viable container port. The expanded use and level of acceptance of this dynamic breakthrough in the shipment of goods has terminated the revolutionary phase of its promotion. Import-export trade has demonstrated quite clearly that both shippers and receivers want the container: the list of commodities it can carry seems almost limitless and other benefits abound. The principal advantage to the transportation industry of the use of systems based on the intermodal freight container lies in the potential for increased productivity of capital, coupled with reduced labour costs. For equivalent cargo throughputs, the capital costs for container ports are lower than the capital costs for conventional break-bulk facilities.
Of far greater significance, however, is the dramatic increase, through mechanization, of labour productivity. Estimates indicate that labour at a container port is between 7.5 and 15 times more productive in terms of cargo volume than labour at a comparable conventional
Vancouver National Harbours Board port. An equally dramatic decrease is realized in the time required for ship to port transfers of cargo. This is important, as all the time a vessel is tied up in port unloading, the person using the transportation facility incurs costs. So unloading time is an important aspect of containerization. Similar savings can be realized on ocean transport costs through the use of large, high-speed container ships: the sizeable capital costs are more than offset by the economies of scale associated with large vessels and by the increased utilization of container ships resulting from significant reductions in transit and in-port times.
Because of the lowering of costs incurred at interchange points, opportunities for alternative transportation routings are increased with the adoption of container transport systems. Direct ship service between Europe and the Far East by services incorporating a North American land bridge could reduce the total distance by about 2,500 miles. Of course, any system using this land bridge would need to be highly automated and organized. Ships would bring cargoes to our east coast ports, those cargoes would be transferred to unit trains or similar trains, taken across the continent and loaded on other ships. Another example would be the provision of container feeder services to smaller ports from major container facilities, possibly offering a better service than could be achieved through the continued use of conventional shipping.
The shipper of cargo benefits through the security and structural protection provided by the container. Substantial reductions in damage and cargo loss result in greater reliability and a potential for reduced insurance costs. In addition, shipping costs are lowered in many instances because of a reduced requirement for protective packaging of cargo within the container. The advantages of containerization have far outweighed the disadvantages and dramatic increases in the use of containers by the developed nations of the world have been observed over the last few years. At Canadian ports, container handlings have increased in the short space of six years from 8,700 20-foot equivalents handled in 1967 to 316,000 20-foot equivalents handled in 1972. Last year's figures and future projections are equally impressive and encouraging.
The success of containerization in both our international and domestic trades will depend upon a number of factors, including the regulatory environment, container rate structures, competition from existing conventional facilities and possible use by external markets of our facilities. Certainly the publication of private documents relating to agreements between the National Harbours Board and private companies will not help the port of Vancouver exploit the manifest benefits that can accrue to Canada in this regard.
I would now like to move into an area of containerization that concerns all of us, that is, its impact on Canada-United States trade. In this regard there can be no question that Canada is finding herself in an increasingly advantageous position relative to her southern neighbour. The proportion of the diversion accounted for by container traffic diversions is not known but is thought to be significant. Furthermore, it has been suggested that diversion of United States container traffic through Canada could increase in the 1970s. United States imports and exports are attracted to Canadian routes because of fast transit

Vancouver National Harbours Board
times, reliability in transportation services, lower rates due to more flexible rate structures applied on Canadian routes and the aggressive marketing policies followed by Canadian port authorities. Among the rate advantages on Canadian routes is the availability of volume rates for rail transportation which offer significant reductions for shipments of over 200 containers per week. The lower rates reflect the higher utilization of equipment and, hence, lower costs associated with larger volume. In general, however, trade diversion between Canada and the United States is a cyclical phenomenon. In any case, the existence of alternative routes outside the home country places some competitive restraint on rates charged to cargo shippers.
I must emphasize that the development of containerization has been assisted considerably in Canada by the maintenance of a relatively regulation-free environment for transportation activities. Multimodal transportation companies are not prohibited under Canadian legislation. The integration of transportation services through such companies has simplified the provision of complete door to door transportation to Canadian shippers. In this case we have a transportation system which can deliver from door to door in Canada, handled by only one carrier.
The shipper also benefits from the effective use of a single, through bill of lading and the simplicity of a single through rate. The development of integrated transportation services is also assisted through the existence of a single body for the regulation of all modes of transportation whose stated aim is the co-ordination of transportation services.
We are looking at a situation here where we have to decide whether we are going to make public the cost inputs of the National Harbours 3oard, revealing these to other ports with which the board might be competing. There is an old saying that Eaton's doesn't tell Simpsons. I think that is the situation here: one port does not want to reveal its input costs to another. In circumstances where there is no competition, this would not be a factor. In my own constituency I am familiar with the input costs of operating the Tobermory-South Bay Mouth ferry and ports maintained by the Department of Public Works. These documents are necessary to determine the viability and practicality of establishing a new ferry service between the port at the west end of Manitoulin Island, Meldrum Bay and Detour, Michigan. These figures are available because they are not in competition with any other country or company; there is not the competitive factor to be taken into consideration.
With regard to the port of Vancouver on the west coast, we are trying to develop a more effective port which handles more goods and services, including containerization. For this reason I am sympathetic with the view expressed by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport that these private, internal input costs should not be made public because of the disadvantageous position in which it would put that port vis-a-vis ports in the United States with which it is in competition.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPIES OF CONTRACTS BETWEEN VANCOUVER HARBOURS BOARD AND CERTAIN FIRMS RESPECTING USE OF PIERS IN 1973 AND 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the motion before us. From time to time in this

House we debate requests for the production of papers. I suppose motions like this are as old as parliament itself, and the process is about the same; many motions are placed on the order paper which would prove very detrimental if accepted and the information made public. Nearly everyone in this House has a reasonable knowledge of transportation costs in a country the size of ours and some of the difficulties we face whether on the basis of regionalism or nationalism. Any information made public that would tend to increase costs and prevent competitiveness on the part of Canadian companies, cities or transportation facilities would only make matters worse for Canadian business in general. We must remember that these businesses pay taxes as well as their employees.
When speaking to a motion such as the one before us we are not just dealing with the companies mentioned in the motion or the National Harbours Board as it pertains to Vancouver harbour; we are speaking about jobs for Canadians. Hon. members are quite familiar with the operations of many Crown corporations. There is a large one in my constituency. It pays grants in lieu of taxes to the municipality in which it is located. At times when I have asked about particular information I have been informed that this type of information is not made public. I am given very good reasons for this, and I accept them.
Looking at the history of transportation in Canada, I think we have come a long way. We have developed new companies and techniques in order to stay in this highly competitive market. Any information made public about the port of Vancouver might be detrimental to the operations of the National Harbours Board, the exportation of Canadian goods and the importation of goods. It would be not only detrimental to the Vancouver area but to a large area-indeed, to Canada in general.
What are some of the competitive factors with which we have to live? We are selling over 15 million tons of coal a year to Japan, and I understand that Japan has built special ships to carry this coal to factories where they manufacture products competitive with our own. This has an effect, of course, on the amount of traffic in imported goods which flows from the port of Vancouver. The enterprising Japanese community has also built ocean-going ships specifically to carry logs. They carry timber to Japan, where it is made into plywood and veneers and brought back to Canada and the United States where it is sold more cheaply than we could manufacture it at home.
I do not think the Canadian public would support an attempt to give out information which would, for example, help the city of Seattle to compete more favourably with the city of Vancouver. Hon. members have heard from two of my hon. friends sound and logical objections to the motion before us. I wish to endorse the position taken by those speakers. We are rot dealing here with any partisan issue but with an issue which has a direct economic effect on Canada in general and Vancouver in particular. No one, surely, would wish to see the government establish a precedent which might be dangerous in the future and seriously hamper the efficiency and freedom of not only the National Harbours Board but of Crown corporations in general. Those corporations having been set up to operate in a businesslike manner, it is surely the duty of parlia-

ment to back their efforts and make sure they are protected and placed in a position to conduct their affairs in an honest and profitable manner.
I do not wish to speculate as to the dire consequences which could result from a decision that operating schemes negotiated between the National Harbours Board and private companies could be made public. The only way in which the National Harbours Board at Port of Vancouver, and other ports for that matter, can remain productive is for their operating agreements with private companies to remain confidential in the interest of preserving competitive advantage. If a Crown corporation happens to be located in a particular community, the community will not object to receiving grants in lieu of taxes. These books are audited. Does General Motors in Oshawa pay taxes to all the communities surrounding Oshawa, or does it pay taxes to Oshawa alone?
It seems to me to be futile to make public declarations which would not create a better opportunity to compete with the maximum impact on the international market related to port traffic. To back up this statement I should like to remind hon. members that 25 cents of every dollar Canadians have in their pockets today comes from international trade. For this reason the National Harbours Board plays a very important role in getting goods out of Canada as well as in bringing goods in from other countries.
For all its excellence in the provision of port facilities, Canada does not hold a copyright of expertise and efficiency in harbour operation. We must continue to improve our facilities so as to remain competitive with other countries in the world, in particular on the west coast where competition can become intense. It would be foolish to take action which would fetter our freedom to compete successfully for the cargo traffic which comprises such an important part of our transportation system.
In addition to the principle of confidentiality which is involved here, the motion contains a practical flaw. Information is a delicate commodity and is useful only if it fits the purpose. It is easy to have too much information and not enough knowledge.
In calling it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the House to the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) who is sponsoring this motion has not been in the House during the course of my speech.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather glad that I am speaking after the dinner break, because a speech immediately following one by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) would be a hard act to follow. It was an excellent act: the style was great, he waxed magnificently in eloquence and delivery but he waned badly in content. In the first half of his oration he attacked his former friends in the party to our left, the members of the NDP. Like a rejected, jilted lover he cajoled and pleaded for a reconciliation. Perhaps the reconciliation has been made; time will tell.
He claimed annoyance that the NDP consider themselves the only people in Canada to be the protectors of the individual rights of Canadians. He says that his party has been against profiteering for a long time. I ask him where, and when? Perhaps he is suffering from selective amnesia, for he seems to have forgotten that his party brought forth a policy to increase the profits of manufacturing through the corporate tax incentives of the last budget. Perhaps he does not understand what it is his colleagues have been saying. They have been saying what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) indicated in Winnipeg in the last week in April when he denied there was any corporate rip-off; the minister said that profits were being properly used to expand capacity, output and jobs. Perhaps he did not understand the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) when he indicated there was no profiteering on a general basis in Canada.
What the minister of Regional Economic Expansion said was mainly an attack on his former friends of the New Democratic Party. But then I think he misconstrued something in his bout of selective amnesia when dealing with what a member of our party said, indeed what our party has stood for for some time. He said that his party had brought about increased wages for the fishermen of Newfoundland and increased wages generally across Canada, and he thought this was great. He said that the Progressive Conservative Party wants to control wages. As I have suggested, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion suffers from selective amnesia, for indeed he forgot to say how his party has also watched and stood by while prices have risen faster than wages, he forgot to say it was a prices and incomes policy that the Progressive Conservative Party advocated so that prices could be held down.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that an election must be called in the not too distant future. Yesterday we first heard that the Liberal government was going to try to buy the votes of its employees by arbitrarily giving them $500 each, while at the same time failing to bargain in good faith in contracts presently being negotiated with civil servants.

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
The government is offering today 2 per cent to 4 per cent increases for openers, finally settling for 7 per cent to 8 per cent, whereas the cost of living nationally is 10.4 per cent and in Ottawa, where most public servants live, it is 11.4 per cent.
Bill C-29, which allegedly deals with profiteering, is in reality a bill dealing with prices and profit margins. These two actions, along with a public-paid junket by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last weekend, indicate, to me at least, blatant pre-election politicking. The new rules of procedure in the House which were introduced, and the supposedly better committee system which has been set up, as a result of which the government would have plenty of time to introduce bills and allow for public scrutiny for a week or two between first and second readings, are once again being short-circuited as this government rushes to put supposedly attractive legislation on the order paper for debate less than 48 hours later.
This government is not interested in governing for the betterment of Canada and Canadians. It is using its authority and power for blatant politicking, trying to put the Liberal Party ahead of the interests of Canadians, merely trying to hang on to power and thus perpetuate itself in office. Unconscionable, undoubtedly; but the Canadian public will not be fooled, for they are intelligent and will think of this bill as the cosmetic farce that it really is. It falls into the same type of political manoeuvre as the announcing of a Lake Ontario park in Tronto by the Secretay of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) during the last election, the increasing of wages for the armed forces which was announced during the last election, and even the announcement of the Minister of Finance of redevelopment of Ottawa's historic marketplace, again made during the last election. Where has the government been for the last 18 months, Mr. Speaker? Under what bush has the Liberal Party been lost? Lost in what forest? For surely they cannot see the forest for the trees. Behind whose skirt has the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs been hiding, or should I say jostling for position with the Prime Minister?
Here we have a government which has faltered in its handling of the economy for some six years now, bouncing from pillar to post like a drunken sailor first during this parliament's encouragement of higher profits in the manufacturing industries in order to bring more investment through the corporate tax concessions of the last budget and now with a bill allegedly to control profits, or excess profits. Which is it they really want, as they speak out of both sides of their mouth at the same time? For the last 18 months, since the people of Canada gave notice to the government on October 30, 1972, of their dissatisfaction, the inept handling of the economy has led to a virtual raping of the low and middle-class wage earners' ability to maintain a decent standard of living.
Inflation, which was just over 5 per cent 18 months ago, has rocketed to the uncharted waters of 10 per cent, and now the government, with its own report tabled Tuesday by the Minister of Finance saying that the worst is yet to come, has finally awakened from its arrogant cocoon to say that it must do something about inflation. This is something the Progressive Conservative Party has been

saying for well over a year in crystal-clear terms. What a half-hearted, timid approach. The government says this bill is a new instrument in its line of defence against inflation. What other instrument does the government have, and what is its line of defence? What other antiinflationary policy has this government espoused? I suggest there is none. The only thing the government has done is introduce some measures to relieve the painful symptoms of those who need relief from the pain of the inflation the government has allowed to run out of control.
I say that Bill C-29 is on one hand a timid, half-hearted approach, while on the other hand it is unconscionably dangerous, severe and autocratic. Indeed, on the one side it is timid and is, allegedly, to deal with profits only, with possibly some selective rollbacks, and I emphasize the word "possibly". This government now, some 18 months late, is talking about controls, a freeze on prices and rollbacks, when our party long ago advanced a prices and incomes policy not dealing just with profits but with dividends, rents, salaries, wages and prices. Even the NDP, the timid tigers of this parliament, have gone further than this Liberal government now proposes. That party has for some time talked about price rollbacks and selective controls even though it has not put forward a completely progressive program.
I should point out that last year both the International Monetary Fund and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development suggested that Canada should introduce a prices and incomes control policy. The International Monetary Fund, in September, 1973 said:
Besides cooling off their economies through use of their federal budgets and control of money and credit, nations should supplement these anti-inflationary tools with wage-price controls or other policies affecting income.
In addition, it stated:
-wage increases were likely to remain high in Canada in the absence of any official action to directly control them.
In December, 1973, the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development stated that Canada's over-all rate of inflation for 1974 would be higher than in 1973, and that inflation in Canada had developed a momentum of its own and could only be offset by a concerted anti-inflation program. Further, it reported that no such program existed in Canada and that inflationary psychology was so solidly entrenched that Canada needed a comprehensive antiinflation program that included wage and price controls if inflation was to be licked.
On the other hand, as I have said, this law is too dangerous, severe and autocratic. This legislation on profiteering would make bad law because it is imprecise; it does not say who the law will effect. An accused would not even know he was accused until the government, acting on information provided by those it had appointed to look into price increases, declared the law to be in effect. As a matter of fact, there is some suggestion that this legislation could be retroactive.
This legislation is penal law, and penal laws are interpreted in the strictest manner by our courts, in line with our democratic philosophy that we as a free people are free to do whatever we wish unless it is explicitly prohibited by law. If this ever became the law of the land, I doubt whether there would be a successful prosecution

and it is doubtful if there would ever be any imprisonment. This bill could well be interpreted as a denial of natural justice under which a person is entitled to know in advance what the law is, to know what charge he is facing, to know, prior to the hearing, the case against him, and to be represented at his trial which should be open to the public and to the press.
This proposed legislation by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is not explicit as to what the law will be. It lacks definition as to what the article is. It does not define "customary" profits, and it does not explain what is an "excess" profit. It gives no idea what the base price would be or what might be an appropriate profit margin. How would a person or corporation charged under this legislation know what the law was and what had to be avoided? The fact is that a company probably would not know what the charge was, whether it was profiteering through inflating prices, too high a mark-up, or whether it had lowered irresponsibly its cost of production because it became inefficient.
As this legislation is proposed, it would discourage a company from becoming efficient and perhaps increasing its profits, because the profit margin that was set would be increased and the company might be prosecuted, whereas a company which is inefficient could charge more for its goods in order to receive the same profit margin. It is suggested that this law could be hashed out in what is really a secret, star chamber cabinet meeting. The fact that a case could possibly be put to the cabinet, sitting as sort of judge and jury without the company or person knowing, with no provision for representations to be made on behalf of the company or person before the cabinet or executive body, is also wrong; it is a denial of the principle of natural justice for the cabinet to wear three hats, one as informant, one as prosecutor and one as judge. This proposed legislation is autocratic and it is wrong.
Why does this government, now 18 months late, bring forth a bill that is badly drafted, ill-conceived and largely unworkable in its present form? If it feels it can calm the people of Canada with cosmetic legislation, it is wrong. The Progressive Conservative Party and, I believe, the voters are too wise for that. This bill, as has been explained by others before me, deals only with a portion of those things which are causing inflation today. It deals only with unidentified articles, whatever they may be. It does not deal directly with services, housing, rents, incomes-all major factors in our ever escalating cost of living. This bill could well prove to be a bureaucratic nightmare.
Even the Liberal Party has not tried to tell us how this bill fits into the over-all philosophy or direction they are aiming for. It is floundering around, attempting to reach out and clutch at something, anything; the government knows not what. At best, it could be considered a vague, ill-conceived attempt to do something about inflation, but one knows not what for sure. It should have been introduced as a budgetary measure, if it is really to be what the government claims, that is, an anti-inflation measure, with possible taxing provisions, in view of the fact that it does have an impact on the country's economy and business and investment communities. The government is not even sure what this bill is designed for. The government,
Profiteering Practices
and the minister who introduced this bill and is responsible for it, can only give legalistic, clause by clause statements as to how it might work.
As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and others have said, there have been no policy statements of any significance or depth to which we can look to see how, or if, this bill will ever be put into force. I note there is no certainty as to when the bill will be proclaimed and no statement of assurance as given in the election expenses act. In fact, this bill, if it were to pass, could stay on the statute books for years and never be proclaimed as the law of the land. If the bill were to become part of our law, it would be left open as to when, if ever, it might be proclaimed.
At the very last, the bill needs a time limit on it, and expiry date of, say, 18 months or two years after its proclamation so that if the government of the day wanted it to continue it would have to seek parliament's approval. If this bill by some miracle ever gets to committee, it needs drastic changes by way of amendment. This should be done only after this House is given more guidance as to the government's intentions for this country which, hopefully, will be revealed in the forthcoming budget.
If this bill should go to the committee it should be noted that clauses 7, 8 and 9 are directly related to Bill C-7 which is now in committee. These two bills should be consolidated or at least considered jointly in Committee. The clauses which relate to offences under the Combines Investigation Act and changing the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission to a more powerful Trade Practices Commission should be dealt with at one time. The bill should be expanded to include services and housing. Services have been included in Bill C-7: why have they not been included here?
In respect of the clause dealing with natural justice, all inquiries under this legislation should be conducted in public. This bill is vague, as I have indicated. I do not think there could be a successful prosecution or any imprisonment whatsoever. Bill C-29 is expected to be referred to the committee on justice and legal affairs, whereas Bill C-7 is before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. If this bill should ever go to committee, it should be considered by the committee that is considering Bill C-7 and at the same time.

Profiteering Practices

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member. Once again, he admits that we are right. He confirmed what I said namely that the bill, from a certain procedural point of view, was too difficult or too hard on the citizens. On the other hand, the NDP member stated that it was not hard enough. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it must be another one of those fine measures, as advocated by the philosophy of the Liberal party, which tries to find natural justice in a middle course.
For months, Mr. Speaker, we were told that the Food Prices Review Board, the Plumptre Board, was not strong enough, had not the necessary coercive powers to be efficient. Amendments were introduced. It would perhaps have been advisable then to carry the amendments and grant coercive powers. However, we did not want to follow that policy. We thought that the people indulging in fraudulent and profiteering practices to make profits understood they could not take advantage of the conditions in the country.
Today, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) upholds a bill to meet requirements made by opposition members, particularly the NDP. Today, they say this is a timid and complicated measure. They suggest there is no authority to freeze prices. To suggest things like that is to distort the facts. Provision is made in the act that the government can at some point declare that prices are immediately frozen. The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) is opposed to that because he suggests that it might be too strong a discretionary power in the hands of a government.

On the other hand, the NDP do not see any real power in the hands of anyone. And that freeze for 30 days, Mr. Speaker, will be followed by inquiries and could in instances of non-compliance be followed by injunctions from the courts. If a company or its directors are found guilty of profiteering the act states that they are liable to fines of up to $10,000 and, if required, to imprisonment for up to two years. I for one feel that that is going quite far. And if NDP members are not satisfied all they have to do is to move on second reading that the fine be increased from $10,000 to a maximum of $50,000, or $100,000, if they can manage to convince all hon. members that the $10,000 fine is inadequate. If they feel that the present term is inadequate they can try and move amendments.
Hon. members will have an opportunity to improve the bill. But to say that it does not provide for any penalty and any authority for enforcement, that it is toothless is I think an exaggeration. This bill goes as far as saying that if a company or a director is found guilty of profiteering and found guilty by the commission they will be paying back the excess profits to the consumers. If this were to prove impractical because, for instance, an individual or a company having charged 3 cents too much on each tin of canned tomatoes sold in Canada it would be difficult to reimburse 3 cents to each consumer, the government could then order the manufacturer or the officials of the company to pay the government the excessive profits, in addition to incurring possible personal fines and prison terms.

To those circumstances we owe the fact that even today we have a bill capable of stirring a salutary fear in industry, as well as bringing to their knees those who are too stiff-necked. The reform presented yesterday by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) offers the advantage of not doing away with what already exists; for example, the Plumptre board will go on with its work.
On the basis of a report of an inquiry commission, the Cabinet will have the power, through an official proclamation, to freeze temporarily the price of some given article and request intervention by the director of research and inquiries. After investigation, the director will submit the evidence to the new Trade Practices Commission, which in turn will have the power to put an end to the objectionable trade practice and to force the supplier to roll back the prices or to refund customers or, if this is not feasible, to pay to the Crown its surplus profits.
Mr. Speaker, this bill must be examined, but both opposition parties refuse to give it second reading to amend it. We do not think this bill is perfect. The hon. member for York South said that its operation seems too complex.
If such is the case, it can be improved at the committee stage. But what we want, and I think we all agree on that, is to catch as soon as possible those who take advantage of the situation and make excessive profits.
I do not understand why the bill cannot be studied in committee and amended. The procedure may be complicated but on the other hand we must be careful. One should not convict everybody in advance and without trial.
The corporations as well as their directors have a right, like every citizen, to present their case before being convicted. That is why they are called to appear before the commission. I do not agree with the NDP theory that they must be convicted more or less without trial, without knowing exactly their position.
I think that the rights of citizens apply to everyone, the poorest as well as the richest, because we are all equal before the law in Canada and that is why we prefer to live here.
On the other hand, there are certain points which could be clarified. Dissatisfaction has been voiced because the bill excludes certain services. However it must be understood that they are services and often we have absolutely no control over services.
Let us take the example of bus tickets. The price of tickets is determined by the transport commissions. The federal commission cannot intervene in an area of provincial jurisdiction.
The same thing applies in the area of trucking, hospital services, telephone rates and other public services. It would not be appropriate for a federal commission to intervene in areas of provincial jurisdiction. If there are abuses it is up to the provincial governments to take their responsibilities.
Reference has also been made to housing. To my mind, the legislation covers also the field of housing, and profiteering on building materials, for instance, would then be corrected.
Profiteering Practices
On the other hand, the housing problem has many elements that cannot be controlled by such a commission. For instance, wage earners have negotiated collective agreements, approved by provincial governments. It would be improper, by passing federal legislation, to try to intervene in those areas which have a strong impact on housing costs.
The same can be said of utilities related to housing: water and sewers. Such services are often provided by municipalities and these are autonomous. It is not the role of federal government to tell municipalities what to do in their own jurisdiction.
However, as I have said, if this measure can be improved upon, let us give the House at least the opportunity to do so by sending this bill to committee after second reading. Notably in the speeches of our friends at the far right of the House, the New Democrats,-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Of the far left-

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Of the far left. No, they are sometimes confused; one would not know.
Benefits are all they talk about. Such company made 25, 30, 40 or 50 per cent more profits than the year before, but that does not mean anything or almost, because for instance a company whose capital would have yielded 40 per cent in 1972 would have made excess profits. The same company which, the following year, 1973, would have had profits of 36 per cent would effectively have suffered a 10 per cent decrease and would still be making excess profits. So the fact that the company received less profit would not be a good enough reason not to submit it to the control of the board.
On the other hand, if the profits of a company amounted to 2 per cent of its capital in 1972 and to 4 per cent the following year, that means there was an increase of 100 per cent, but it would not be considered sufficient.
We must therefore stop using slogans such as those, to be fair to everyone. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands suggested, we should consider the return on the capital, not only the profit realized compared with the preceding year.
Even then, there could be hidden facts. Excessive profits might have been hidden in the figures of executive salaries or in inflated advertising contracts or subcontracts which could be a temporary camouflage of the profits of the company. Mr. Speaker, the opposition baffles me. Frankly, I am rather disappointed to see that opposition members do not even want to give the House an opportunity to study the bill.
The leader of the NDP, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), has said that this legislation is a last minute sop offered to the NDP. Mr. speaker, we are not afraid of an election. We were returned to office in 1973, and everyone predicted that we would not last one week. Now we have been here for a year and a half, and we have not "sopped" anybody. We have passed good law for the benefit of Canadians, and that is why we are still here today.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
In a time of inflation the people of Canada want the members of this House to do their best. They want us to try to cope with the problem, as we are doing through this bill. But if hon. members opposite cause an election, we will not mind. We will be back on this side. We are not afraid of that. The government is fully dressed, fully prepared with this piece of legislation. It is the NDP that has been caught naked, with its pants down. Its members are unwilling streakers. They are not really prepared to accept effective legislation.
Canadians want the government to crack down on pricegouging practices. This legislation provides the necessary powers, machinery and penalties. Why are the members of the NDP so upset because the government is doing its job? As usual they are all talk. They are afraid of losing one of their handy slogans. They could not continue to barrage the Canadian public with inflated verbal rip-offs. Slogan politics fall apart when faced with effective government action.
The government has every intention of using the new powers proposed under this bill to protect the Canadian consumer from unfair trade practices. But, Mr. Speaker, we do not intend to go on a witch-hunt. I recognize that business depends on profits for growth and investment. This bill does not outlaw profits. It gives the government the power to freeze and roll back prices where suppliers are taking unfair advantage of the consumer. A businessman is entitled to profit but he has no right to use the present situation to abuse the consumer. We will put those guys in their places with this bill. Both the Conservatives and the NDP want to go in another direction. The answer of hon. members opposite is to freeze everything but they opposed the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) when he gave an increase to the civil service. They said what he was proposing was not enough. Others said it was far too much. Hon. members opposite have their own internal problems.
I think that this piece of legislation is good. Of course, it is not perfect and we are willing to discuss amendments, but the public should not be left with the impression that there is nothing in this bill. We do not want to create injustices in this country, but we will not permit profiteers to exploit the situation.

speechtext: Who are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Name them.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: If we want to get them, we will get them. We must have inquiries. Of course, the NDP would like us to do things right away. But there must be investigations. Then those found guilty will have to pay a fine or be put in jail. As a result, more people will not abuse the situation. We will always allow a fair margin of profit for business people. They are entitled to that. But we want to get at the gougers, and to do that we want this bill to receive second reading. Then hon. members will have plenty of opportunity to make suggestions for amendments. But the public should not be deceived. Hon. members opposite are afraid of the effectiveness of this bill. That is why they do not want it passed. The people of Canada would then see them in their true light.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister who preceded me suggested that members on this side had not studied the bill. I suggest to him that we have indeed studied it very carefully. We studied it to see if it had anything worth amending in it in the first place. Unfortunately, the bill is so hoary-minded, so vague, so incomprensible in its details that it is not worth sending to committee.
The problems that this country faced prior to October 30, 1972, were inflation, unemployment insurance, the unemployment problem itself, lack of industrial growth, lack of processing of raw materials in this country and development of a nation. The country still faces those problems. We have the answers to solve them and we will let the minister hear those answers on election platforms. And if he is successful and returns to sit in this House in opposition, we will also let him hear them here.
This bill seeks to amend the Combines Investigation Act. It is the second amendment to that act introduced since the Speech from the Throne was delivered last February. The first amending bill, No. C-7, is still before committee. Clearly, if the present bill had been intended to be part of the government's strategy in solving inflation problems, it would have been introduced with the previous bill as one package and would have been introduced earlier this session. But the truth of the matter is that this bill was flung together over a weekend. It was dumped on this House to appease the NDP, to suck them in so they could say they were doing something about profiteers and price gougers. But the members of the NDP are a little smarter than that. Opposition members as a whole are a little smarter than that. The government must think we are pretty foolish if it pretends that this bill will do anything about inflation and price gouging.
We are all interested in stopping profiteering. We are all concerned about inflation. But this bill is merely fluff; it is merely bluff. It does not do anything with respect to these problems. It does not do anything about house prices, about the price of houses already built, for which the materials have already been paid, yet the prices of those houses are raised by as much as $3,000 to $4,000 over one weekend. That may be gouging, that may be an unrealistic price increase and certainly it cannot be treated as cons-cionable, yet this bill does not touch that problem. Actually, it deals with hardly any problems.
What is the bill supposed to attack? It purports, to deal with the price of articles which seriously affect the living costs of all, or a great majority of Canadians. Therefore, the bill applies only to those articles which seriously affect all Canadians, or the great majority of them. A few weeks ago our newspapers spoke of a certain optical company which manufactures eye glasses: it was accused of gouging. Do eye glasses affect the living costs of all, or a great majority of Canadians? I suggest that the majority of Canadians do not wear eye glasses, not even the majority of the members of this House. So eye glasses are not included. The minister who spoke before me mentioned shoes. Are we talking about men's, or women's, shoes? If we mean women's shoes, they certainly do not affect
May 2, 1974

living costs of a great majority of Canadians. Perhaps of half the population, but not the great majority. The same applies to men's shoes. This bill is to affect the price of articles used by all, or a great majority of Canadians. Remember that.
What about the price of bricks? How many Canadians actually use bricks? I suppose those who are thinking of buying or building a house need bricks. But do all Canadians, or the majority, use bricks? No, sir. And what about lumber? Lumber is not included, if we apply the same definition. How many things are included? Food is not. Yet we all eat, I trust.
