subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not accept that suggestion. How can the bill attempt to control the price of agricultural products when it obviously does not cover fertilizer and other things used by the farmer. In fact, it covers hardly any product. This bill does not include very much. It covers only articles which are consumed or used by all, or a great majority of Canadians. That puts a serious limit on the scope of the bill.
What does the bill require? With respect to those articles on which excessive profits are being made, the bill says
Profiteering Practices
that two things must happen. First, the commission or board to be set up must recommend action to the cabinet, and the cabinet must decide if something is seriously wrong. When it is so satisfied, it may invoke the act and direct that guidelines shall be established to deal with the industry or product in question. Remember, it must be a product which is used by all, or the majority of our people. Then the director must inquire as to what action must be taken, then the company involved may be taken to court. That is the sort of bill this is-and this sort of legislation is supposed to control the price of certain articles.
Clearly, as the Globe and Mail said today, this bill is a paper tiger. Earlier today a minister of the government, using all his rhetoric said, "Fellows, why hold the bill up in the House? Would it not be better to send the bill to committee, where it can be fixed." This bill is so bad that we despair of fixing it. The bill is a sham, notwithstanding all the rhetoric of ministers who have spoken today. The government should withdraw the bill. I suspect that after tonight it will be filed away under the table. Probably it will never see the light of day again. It has been shown to be a sham and a sop to win the support of the NDP.
In this country we need some method to control inflation. The government could use several such methods. We have suggested an income policy and a commodities policy under which more commodities would be processed in Canada. As well, we support a monetary policy which would separate our money supply from the New York market. We would attack government expenses. This bill represents the beginning of an incomes policy. Sir, we need a comprehensive incomes policy. Our program would begin with a 60 to 90-day freeze on wages, prices and profits and would be imposed for two reasons. First, it would show the country that we really mean business and that those who are anticipating further price rises are likely to be disappointed. We would want to curb inflationary expectations in society.
Second, we would need time to develop, with the provinces and other bodies, a comprehensive program to control basic costs across the board. That is what our incomes program would involve. We would set up an incomes and prices review board which would set up realistic guidelines to cover wages and salaries, including salaries paid to executives. We would not be concerned only about the poor guy who works on the line but would include the executive who draws a large salary. The board would determine the profit that a company would need to attract further capital and to expand. It would determine what the real input costs are and what the real price structure should be on a fair basis. However, this proposal by the government does not do anything of the kind. The program at the outset suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on a comprehensive basis would probably be for 18 months to two years. It perhaps might even have to be longer than that. Indeed, it might have to become part of a permanent competition policy.
In that regard, may I point out the difference between the philosophy of an incomes policy as prescribed by this party and the woolly, button-down, wing collar approach or look of society as visualized by the government party. We do not live entirely in a marketplace economy. We do

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
not live in an economy of open and complete competition. Certainly some parts are open, in complete competition. Small stores compete with other small stores perhaps; small businesses compete with other small businesses in the same trade, perhaps. But the great part of our industrial might is involved in large organizations that have a monopoly or oligarchy position in our society, where the price they charge for their product does not necessarily bear any true relation to cost.
We have a situation where big industry, big labour and big government are not subject to the marketplace forces of competition. In the past, the answer by the government to this condition has been the Combines Investigation Act. I say that is a useless act in the ultimate. It really has not done anything to affect the oligarchies or to create competition. It may well be-and I will speak about this later- that it is not necessarily desirable in some fields that there be competition. Under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, the only people who have been caught have been stupid. People who make mistakes are caught under that act, but by and large it is only when they make a goof that they are caught.
Prices are charged by big business and big labour on the basis of what the traffic will bear. It is almost ridiculous, but the bill refers to profit margins that are "customarily" obtained. The bill even recognizes that it is all right to have these profit margins. If your profit margin is always 100 per cent, that is all right. But if you make 200 per cent, that is bad even though possibly you should not have made 100 per cent in the first place.
We must recognize the realities of 1974. Big business operates on a price leadership basis. Does anyone here seriously believe there is any competition between our big banks? Just a week and a half ago the Bank of Canada raised the re-discount rate. Suddenly the Royal said, "ten and a half it is," and five other banks instantly said it was 10 Vi per cent. The Commerce took another day and a half to get to 10 Vi per cent for the prime rate. Does anyone believe there is real competition between the banks? The only competition is in the advertising-Susie of the Commerce and little Mary of the Royal Bank.
Is there any real competition in automobiles? Is there any real competition between the oil companies? I was in Saskatchewan recently. I noticed oil company prices posted on the five pumps were about the same as I pay in Ontario. In fact, in one town it was a little more. I happen to be at this end of the pipeline, and they are at the other. The price in the Texaco pump in Mississauga is 59.9 cents a gallon. The refinery is right in Port Credit, in Mississauga. When I travel 60 miles to my cottage, the No. 2 Texaco gasoline, which comes from the same refinery, is
54.9	cents a gallon-what the traffic will bear.
This government has to understand the whole question of competition and the kind of society in which we live. This government is completely out of it. Last fall there was a strike in the oil refinery at Port Credit. I went to see the strikers and talked to them and their union leader. The leader of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union said they were not fighting over money. They had agreed on that. The oil companies and the union had already agreed on the wages for refinery workers. That was agreed in the package. What was the strike about? It was about

safety conditions in that particular refinery, and the way the supervisory force acted. The wages had already been settled. They had been determined by big labour and big business operating in concert, quite able to pass it on right through the system. They are able to do this because of their size.
Within the past week or so we have witnessed an example of price leadership. Many of us applauded the activities of the Steel Company of Canada saying to its union that it was necessary to increase wages for its employees. Immediately, Falconbridge, Inco and Westinghouse increased wages. It went right through the big structures in society. Perhaps it was necessary because of inflation. But what do we have? We have bigness. We have the large, uncontrolled organizations in our society able to do just about what they want.
The purpose of an incomes and prices review board is so that we, the public, have some say because there really is no competition in the market that will control prices. It has been suggested we can control prices by bringing in imports and creating foreign competition. However, when Ford and General Motors have plants in every country, do you really control prices by allowing imports? Not on your life!
We need big corporations, oligarchies and monopolies. There is nothing wrong with Canada having these. After all, Canada is a nation of only 22 million people. It needs an economy on the scale that bigness gives. It needs the R and D expertise that can be developed in big corporations. But there has to be some control over their activities. That control has to be a comprehensive incomes policy applied to the oligarchic and monopolistic situation in our economy. We need something to replace competition. Competition to control these things went out with the wing collar. That is the philosophy of the Liberal Party-wing collar, button-down shirt, dickie and big, starched cuffs. They have not had a new idea in years. They keep bringing in amendments to the Combines Investigation Act.
Big business, large unions combining together can pass on their costs and take all the traffic will bear. They can exact an ever increasing share of the economy. They can use their price leadership and power to take over small corporations. This is part of the reason we need an incomes policy, to make things fair, to give the rest of us more protection against the taking of more and more from the total pot.
An incomes policy is not just an attack on profits. Profits are not the total picture. A small corporation may not make any profit at all. The chief executive may own a yacht and receive a salary of $100,000, but the company may not make any profit. Suppose there is no actual figure below the line, but the controlling corporation in some other country takes a royalty which makes sure that the company concerned never actually makes a profit. The whole picture must be kept in mind, including wages and salaries, including whatever is paid in directors' fees, compensation, royalties and expenses for travel, and so on. The bill before us acknowledges the existing accounting system and says, "As long as you comply with that system,
May 2, 1974

you are all right." The bill does not really get at the problem.
We need a comprehensive policy, a policy which covers, or is capable of covering, the entire system. We need a policy which is not confined to those few articles which are consumed by all Canadians, or by the vast majority of Canadians. After all, we live in an interdependent society and if I get ripped off for glasses, somebody else may get ripped off for a wheelchair. These articles may not be covered by the bill, yet all of them add to my cost of living or to my neighbour's cost of living. So a selective approach of the kind contemplated can do nothing. It is merely window-dressing.
As the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) said, the bill sets up a bureaucracy with a star-chamber procedure; the star-chamber, or commission, is policeman, judge and jury, and it is under the control of a political cabinet. Isn't that a fine state of affairs in a free country? On this basis alone, the bill constitutes an attempt to deny natural justice.
The problem we should be attempting to meet is the menace of inflation. This is the problem which occupies the thoughts of my constituents; this is the topic about which I am continually hearing from those who come to my office, from my employees, frorp my wife. They see the cost of ordinary things going up from week to week. It used to be one could buy a Volkswagen for $1,600. Now the price is $3,200.
Inflation is the challenge, but the bill before us does nothing to meet that challenge. We are asked to send it to committee for second reading. But before this is done, the House must approve the principle, the general design of the bill. And when the general design of the bill is so fraudulent and so misleading, how can it possibly be corrected or improved in committee? Surely the supporters of the government know this. Surely they have read the bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, they know.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: My hon. friend says they know. Mr. Speaker, this bill is proof they are bankrupt of ideas, that they are full of puffery. They know their bill is a fraud and they know their government is a fraud. They have introduced this bill as a last straw to grab at as they prepare to go before the people in a general election. They want to say, "We intended to do something about profiteering and gouging, but the opposition would not let us." Mr. Speaker, they have no intention of doing anything. They know they have no such intention; and even if the bill were proclaimed immediately and action were taken immediately, it would not succeed. After all, the legislation covers only a limited range of articles, and of these government spokesmen have not mentioned one; they have not told us what articles they would go after or what companies they would go after. They have shown no reason for advancing this proposition. The bill is a fraud, the government is a fraud, and the government must go.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) pre-empted the phrase with which I intended to open my contribution to the debate. It was a good phrase, it
Profiteering Practices
aptly describes the situation, and with slight variations I want to use it now. In my view, the legislation before us is a snare, a delusion and a trap and we do not intend to fall into it. It is clear that the legislation is both too little and too late. The barn door has been locked long after the horse has been stolen. Without attempting to go into details of the bill, it seems to me it is cosmetic in nature and designed to win the support of this party at the last minute, and it will not be used in any effective effort to stop inflation or prevent profiteering.
Our leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), in his usual clear and forceful manner exposed the major and overwhelming weaknesses of the bill. I fully agree with his criticism and with his conclusion that we cannot possibly support such a measure. Nor do I think this conclusion requires us to make any apologies for trying to make parliament work as we have over the past 18 months. If I thought for one minute that the bill would work and that it would make any contribution toward solving the problems of inflation or profiteering, I would be glad to support it, but I do not see how I can support a measure which deals so ineffectively with such a crucial subject. We have voted for other government legislation on its merits, and we have voted against government legislation on its merits. I refer to the reduction in the corporation tax as an illustration of this. We will vote against this bill because we do not think it has any merit.
One has to remember, of course, that the wording of the legislation is not all-important. What is important is who is responsible for the enforcement and carrying out of the act. It was pointed out earlier in this debate that the act's enforcement depends entirely on the Liberal cabinet. Its real intent and the real content of the legislation have never been revealed. We have not been told, even in outline, what policy the government intends to adopt in regard to declaring that the bill applies to any article or articles. We are told nothing of this. The procedure is to be based, in part, on reports under the Inquiries Act. At the present time the only authority to make such inquiries is the Food Prices Review Board, whose jurisdiction is confined to food prices. It is true that proposed section 50(2) of the bill gives the governor in council authority to make a declaration, notwithstanding that there is no report and inquiry. But this, as the marginal note to the section says and as the minister himself has said, is only to be employed in cases of emergency for very unusual circumstances.
The key phrase in the act is "exceptionable trade practices". These are partly defined in section 54 as the exacting of "a profit margin on the sale or distribution of the article that is greater than he would customarily obtain on such sale or distribution". The words "customarily obtain" are completely vague. Here again, the government is required to step in and issue guidelines relating to the manner of the determination by the supplier of an article of the profit margin that he would customarily obtain.
However, the government has not seen fit to tell this House what sort of guidelines it has in mind. I have not heard a word about that in this debate. It seems to me to be an insult to parliament to ask parliament to pass legislation conferring wide powers on the government without

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
indicating in any way, shape or form what the government's intentions are with respect to the exercise of those powers. We do not know in what type of cases it proposes to make declarations. Nor do we know its thinking as to the definition of the guidelines which will set the standards to be applied. We are, indeed, being asked to buy a pig in a poke.
I have already mentioned that the important question is, who is responsible for enforcing and carrying out the act? In this case it is in the hands of the government itself as to whether the act will ever be enforced or carried out. The likelihood of its ever being effectively carried out must be considered in light of the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the minister which were recited to the House by the hon. member for York South yesterday.
The minister has told us that in his opinion there has been no profiteering up to the present time, or at any rate no proof of profiteering, and that he only intends to apply the act sparingly and in serious and obvious cases. That alone indicates that there is no intention to enforce this act. This attitude is, of course, on a par with the record of the Liberal Party in this field for generations. A Combines Investigation Act in various forms has been on the statute books for roughly 50 years. Its proposed purpose was to deal effectively with combines and monopolies. Its effectiveness can be judged by the fact that according to "Reynolds on Competition", and to our common knowledge, as well as in the views of other authorities, no modern country has been so ridden with monopolies or oligopolies as Canada.
The legalistic steps provided for in the Combines Investigation Act have turned out to be ineffective. Corporate organizations which are in fact combines have been prosecuted at great expense and with great delay. Even if convictions are registered and fines are paid, a new form of organization has been thought up by some well-informed, astute lawyer, has been established and an effective monopoly has carried on restrictive practices untouched by the legislation.
This bill, like the Combines Investigation Act, shows very little evidence of serious intent behind it. It has glaring gaps and omissions. Services, as has been said before, are not included, and unless the definition in the new competition act is enacted and applied to this act, the act will not apply to housing, interest rates, and many other important services. As the field of services in our economy expands, this means that some of the most important items which enter into the inflation picture are not covered by this measure at all.
The hon. member for York South has said there is no continuing monitoring agency to act in the field of profiteering. This bill, as is obvious to anyone who has read it, is highly complex. It provides for a complex and tangled process which may take months, indeed years, to work out. One starts in the ordinary case with an inquiry. Inquiries are often prolonged. If you hire a good lawyer, he is quite expert at prolonging inquiries. The inquiry is followed by a report, which may in turn be followed by a declaration by the governor in council. Finally, this may lead to a hearing before the Trade Practices Commission and some direction from them.

Involved in the process, of course, is the issue of guidelines. This will be no simple task since the guidelines will presumably be applicable to each class of goods covered. There is ample provision in the act for exemptions by the governor in council. Interim injunctions, which are the only effective method of getting an immediate price freeze, can only be issued as a result of proceedings in the courts. Those with court experience know that you do not get an injunction just like that. The power of the Trade Practices Commission to make a cease and desist order is limited to the stage following the hearing and determination that an exceptionable trade practice has occurred. The Trade Practices Commission has no power to freeze prices while the investigation is going on.
There must be very few of us in this House, Mr. Speaker, who are not conscious that spiralling inflation and the cost of living present to very many Canadians a situation of tragic hardship. I know in my own constituency of rising cost of rentals which has completely eaten away the increases that this parliament voted our old age pensioners and other people dependent on small and fixed incomes. Escalation in accordance with the cost of living, a provision we have legislated, is not sufficient for those who have not the means to buy houses, who cannot pay large rentals and are being forced out of homes that they rent at the present time. Every weekend when I go home I hear of instances of this tragic situation. It is my view, Mr. Speaker, that if we supported this bill we would be deceiving our constituents. We would be building up a hope for them, a hope that would inevitably turn out to be a false hope. I, for one, do not wish to have any part in such a deception.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) made a good, fighting speech this afternoon which we all enjoyed. The only real point that he made was that the opposition parties should accept the bill on second reading and let it go to committee where it could be improved by amendment. The trouble is that he missed the point entirely. This bill is so bad, so amorphous that it cannot be effectively amended in committee. You cannot write a bill in committee, Mr. Speaker; you have to have some principle on which you can graft amendments that are proposed. Committee is a place to improve the details of a bill. It is not a place to write a bill, to put principles into a bill which has none. What is needed is a totally new bill. We need a new start on this effort to deal with profiteering and gouging.
We cannot be asked to accept this bill in principle, because there are no principles in it. Or if there are, they are concealed behind these phrases which nobody in the government has taken the trouble to explain to us. I want to make it abundantly clear that to say this is not to approve of gouging or profiteering. It is to demand that if you go out to fight such an all-pervasive institution as profiteering, you choose weapons that can do the job. This bill is like using a peashooter to destroy a tank: it simply will not work.

I hear hon. members agreeing. However, they do not put forward any alternatives indicating how these terms could be more precisely defined or what these definitions should be. If there were a general system of prices and income controls, which they have been proposing, definitions of base prices and customary profit margins would be required for the entire economy and not just for particular sectors as proposed in this bill. Yet the Conservative members have said nothing about how they would do this, whether by regulation or by definition in the law itself. Instead, they say they would have a general freeze and then they would figure out what to do.
The hon. member complained, also, that there were no discussions about philosophy in the speech by the minister yesterday on second reading. This is not correct. The philosophy was set out in the opening portion of the minister's speech. We all know that the Canadian public wants action more than just philosophy, and that it will not accept and put up with the nonsense put forward so far by the opposition during this debate.
There have been complaints on the part of spokesmen for the Conservative Party on consumer affairs that there has been no action on reports by the Food Prices Review Board, yet the government's decision to put in place special subsidy programs to restrain increases in the price of bread and milk, and the government's decision to advance the timing of the increase in family allowances, came from
Profiteering Practices
recommendations of the Food Prices Review Board. Contrary to what the hon. member for St. John's East said yesterday, bread and milk subsidy programs did restrain increases which otherwise would have taken place. Contrary to what he said, the government has carried out the basic recommendations of the Food Prices Review Board in respect of the egg marketing agency, that is, that a special inquiry be held into the entire operation of the marketing plan. The government gave this task to the Farm Products Marketing Council and the inquiry is under way. Contrary to what the hon. member for St. John's East said yesterday, the bakeries did agree to abide by the Food Prices Review Board findings. They did, in fact, restrain or roll back prices at the request of the minister, on a voluntary basis, to the levels considered acceptable by the Food Prices Review Board.
We also heard the hon. member for St. John's East yesterday speaking against the proposal that the Trade Practices Commission order a profiteer to pay back excess gains. What does the Conservative Party want to do with excess gains? We have not heard any submission on this aspect of the proposals contained in the bill. Having not heard what they want to do with excess gains, I think we are reasonably and legitimately entitled to think that this indicates support by the Conservative Party for big business and for excessive gains.
The final part of the criticism put forward yesterday by the hon. member for St. John's East was in the form of a quotation from Tuesday's Globe and Mail editorial which expressed skepticism about Bill C-29. He evidently forgot to mention that in the same editorial there was complete rejection of the Progressive Conservative proposal for a general system of price and income control.
Yesterday we heard the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and we were rather surprised, I must say, because he either did not understand or did not want to understand what is contained in this bill. For a long time that hon. member has been calling for a means to enable the government to take action against profiteering, but when he and his party are put to the test they reject the chance to enable a bill for this purpose to become law. That hon. member takes the position that no bill and no action is preferable to the government's proposal because he disagrees with some of its details, mainly because of misunderstanding.
The hon. member went on to say that the government does not indicate any intention to use the law it passes, yet the minister in his speech yesterday specifically said just the opposite. If the hon. member for York South really wanted to enable action to be taken against profiteers now, he would support the bill basically in its present form, giving the government the responsibility for using the powers provided in this bill. He would be putting the government's intentions to the test; and if he were not in agreement with the way the government used the law when it should have done so, he and his party could vote no confidence in the government. This would seem to me the more sensible line of approach for the NDP to follow, rather than to prevent even the likelihood of action that is now intended in this very important field of endeavour.
There were comments made yesterday about the question of monitoring price development. The minister did

May 2, 1974
Profiteering Practices
say in his opening remarks that the government was prepared to set up additional boards immediately upon passage of the bill to monitor certain sectors where such action appeared necessary. Contrary to what the member of York South was suggesting yesterday, this government is not proposing to wait for a report of a board of inquiry. If the government has adequate information from other sources, this bill would enable the government to act without waiting for such a report.
Again, contrary to what the hon. member for York South suggested yesterday, the proposed Trade Practices Commission is not, and will not be a part-time commission. The proposal in the bill would enable a sufficient number of full-time members to be available to carry out the work required by the bill, and anyone with eyes to read can look up section 16(1) in the bill which contains the definition of temporary additions. There is definitely a distinction in the English language between "part-time" and "temporary" which perhaps escaped the hon. member for York South who, by the way, seems also to misunderstand the proposal in the bill for dealing with profiteering.
The inquiry and report of a board prior to a declaration, the inquiries by the director and the hearings by the Trade Practices Commission are not the same thing and are not for the same purposes. The inquiry and report by a board prior to a declaration would be about a sector, industry or class of products generally to help provide the kind of general information which would provide a basis for the government to decide on the making of a declaration. The declaration, once made, and accompanied by or including the three notification procedures and definitions of customary profits, would immediately create a 30-day freeze on the products covered and would create the legal obligation that all suppliers of the products not sell them at prices that would cause the customary profit guidelines to be exceeded.
The procedure set out in the act for inquiry by the director, the hearings and orders by the Trade Practices Commission, would be the procedure required to enable appropriate accumulative, punitive action to be taken against individual suppliers who do not live up to the legal requirements created by the declaration, guidelines and regulations. There must be some procedure for determining who is not meeting the requirements of the guidelines and regulations-a good, sound and fair procedure-in connection with a declaration and for then going on to impose the sanction of the law against that person. Our system of law must ensure that the alleged lawbreaker has a hearing before the sanction of the law is imposed on him. This is the purpose of the inquiry by the director and the hearings by the commission.
The hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) yesterday stressed very well the necessity and importance in principle of this kind of approach in our legal system. The director's inquiry would determine whether there is evidence of an offence sufficient to bring the matter before a body which could make a decision about it. The bill does set out the kind of approach the hon. member for York South said is necessary. I quote from page 1946 of Hansard where he is recorded as having said:
When a thorough but quick inquiry is made and a price increase is

found to be unjustified, there must be immediate authority to tell the company that they cannot increase their price.
Those are the words of the hon. member for York South. This is the effect of a declaration with accompanying prenotification requirements and customary profit margin guidelines. Once they are provided, they would apply to all firms selling the category of goods at the level of distribution mentioned in the declaration, and not just one firm.
The hon. member for York South was completely wrong yesterday when he said that the bill does not give the government, a commission or anyone the power to freeze prices for 30 days. These powers are spelled out in section 51 very clearly. No one could raise the price without first giving the required notice up to 30 days and this means, as the section says, a freeze for the period of the notice.
With regard to the method of determining or defining the customary profit margins, the government never said that one should compare current profits only with the immediately preceding year. The speech made by the minister yesterday suggested the opposite approach. The example used was just a hypothetical one for the sake of explaining the matter, but evidently it was not understood. The hon. member for York South is concerned that it would be up to the government to decide whether a declaration should be made to bring the powers of the act into force for any class of article or sector. Surely such an authority to intervene in the economy with what possibly could be disruptive effects must be in the hands not of an appointed body but one accountable to the public through parliament.
This approach very often has been raised as one of the basic principles in our democracy. Very often we hear members opposite complain about the fact that there are too many bodies not directly responsible for their actions to parliament except once a year when they appear before the committee. Here the government has met that criticism in sections 51, 52 and 53 by saying it should be the decision of the governor in council and that this power should not be made available to a body removed from parliament itself.
If action had to be taken automatically on the request of an appointed board, what would the NDP say if the board was not willing to make the kind of recommendation that parliament and the public generally felt would be required? The NDP would be the first to object to this approach. The NDP criticism, unfortunately, means that the government should not be given the power to take action against profiteering, something directly opposed to what the NDP claims is necessary for the protection of the public. In conclusion-and this is a very sad conclusion because we had thought a matter of this importance, in the interests of the Canadian people, would have received support from all sides of the House-I can only say it is my distinct impression that the Canadian people will not take lightly the fact that both the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party backed off with excuses when the crunch came to deal with profiteering in a serious and responsible manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words about

the bill before us because I think it is tremendously important. 1 also think that it might not be necessary to discuss it because even if it were passed, this bill would not remedy the situation or save the victims of the system.
Mr. Speaker, even if this bill is not really important it is considered as such. At least it is very important for the New Democrats. I think myself that it is a minor issue but the government intends to prevent some businesses from making undue profits. We have to define profits and establish who makes such big profits, who will be taxed, who is responsible. Mr. Speaker, if this bill were comprehensive, it would benefit the whole economic sector and the whole business system. This bill will cover only some of the citizens while others who might be making 100, 200, 1000 times more profits will not be affected at all.
Mr. Speaker, any legislation must be as fair as possible. I find this measure unfair because it does not meet our needs.
The bill before us should include some provisions to lower prices and the cost of living at the consumer and producer level. If we want the cost of living to be reduced at the consumer level, it must first be reduced at the producer level.
And the cost of production is increasing, as it has always increased because of various factors, economic factors particularly, which are attributable to the governments, since several governments are involved in this "economic affair".
Mr. Speaker, if we really want to have just and reasonable laws, we shall never achieve our aim by imposing surtaxes on those who make profits to develop their business, and create new institutions. If we prevent them from making certain profits, we shall also be preventing them from developing, and when they need this development, they will be told to go to the Industrial Development Bank and borrow at 12 per cent, or to go to the new Business Development Bank that we are now establishing, where they will again borrow at an interest rate of 12 or 13 per cent. There is undoubtedly no limit to this type of thing. Therefore, the intention is to restrict profits by other means, but not to restrict the action of the government, and more specifically that of the Industrial Development Bank or of the new bank which will be established, or of all the financial institutions which make undue profits and exploit Canadians. Let us compare these profits with those of companies or associations. Who do we want to tax now? Whose profits do we want to cut? It is easy to see that other institutions depend on them and make two or three times as much profits, and even more. These institutions are not bothered, they are sacred, holy.
Yet all that boosts the cost of living because the manufacturing companies that make profits are indirectly financed by the financial institutions. Financial institutions make profits, not companies involved in production. They are the ones that deal with the capital, make the capital, handle the capital and turn in the profits. This is where the money and the profits go. This is what nobody attacks!
Mr. Speaker, we should like to be on the side of those who support this bill; we do not object completely to the bill, but we know that we work for nothing. We know that
Business of the House
what we are doing will not matter at all, that it will not improve economic conditions but will worsen them. Mr. Speaker, the more we cling to the present system, the more we support and enforce it, the more we contribute to the imbalance of the economy. The more also we thus contribute to inflation, rising prices and the increased cost of living.
Inflation is due to the fact that the financial system is not consistent with the realities of production or consumption. The monetary accounting of the system is wrong and only honest accounting would correct inflation without being prejudicial to the legitimate individual interests. We would need an accounting consistent with reality. This would entail the application of financial data stated by the economic expert C. H. Douglas fifty years ago and known under the name of Social Credit. If those financial data had been applied, such a reform would have avoided many troubles to the people.
Mr. Speaker, if the rise in price shows that the system is lacking and should the financial system were in accordance with reality, not only would there be no inflation but on the contrary prices would gradually decrease as technical progress and manufacturing processes would facilitate production.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

HOUSING-NEWFOUNDLAND-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION PROGRAM TO RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is customary I want to state that my reason for rising at this time is to try to impress on members of the House the need to emphasize the question that I put to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) on April 15. It had to do with the announcement of the minister to extend the residential rehabilitation program for housing beyond the restricted policy under the act to qualify citizens in neighbourhood improvement areas.
When the minister gave us particulars regarding the new rural and native housing program under which some
50,000	homes would be built over the next five years to enable citizens within that category to build a house in rural areas, he stated that under that new policy citizens in rural communities would qualify beyond the provisions of the National Housing Act. Furthermore, the new rural and native housing program would allow citizens in rural communities to take advantage of the residential rehabilitation program. I can only say that this program would benefit my constituents, and that it is certainly what is required.
With regard to the original program, I have been one of the minister's most staunch supporters in the introduction of this program and even more so when he extended the program to those in rural Canada, because it lifted the restriction which required those benefitting under the program to live within a neighbourhood improvement area which had to be designated by the province concerned. Furthermore, only $J0 million was provided for this program across Canada, and for Newfoundland only some $660,000 was provided. I mention this because the housing situation in Newfoundland can only be classified as disastrous.
It is obvious to everyone that with rates of interest advancing it will be almost impossible for those on low incomes to acquire new homes. But as is provided by the amendments to the act, this program would provide an opportunity for those living in substandard homes to improve the condition of their homes, homes which are deteriorating due to the fact that with the cost of building materials rising because of inflation the occupants on the lowest income scale cannot afford to improve them. I maintain that every effort should be extended to make funds available to allow every Canadian falling within this category to take advantage of the $5,000 loans available, with the forgiveness of $2,500 if their income falls below or is equal to $6,000, and beyond that to reduce the forgiveness by $1 for every $2 of income in excess of $6,000.
I realize that the minister is restricted in directing this program until agreements are signed with the provinces and until minimum standards are laid down by municipalities or by the provinces. But when I am overburdened with letters from constituents begging me for assistance to improve their homes it is most frustrating that these restrictions exist. I can show you, Mr. Speaker, from applications made to housing corporations in my district, that literally thousands of citizens are living in

the most precarious circumstances even beyond the control and the ability of those who are designated to help. It becomes a frustrating experience trying to help alleviate a problem which is beyond anyone's power to control.
If I can use only one example, one does not have to go beyond increases in the cost of home heating oil. Citizens on welfare, who live mainly in substandard homes, cannot even cope with the cost of fuel, especially in the winter months. And the provinces are unable to cope with the cost of the increase in home heating oil beyond the increases which are extended to citizens through social assistance. I therefore suggest that the residential rehabilitation program should be extended to provide insulation for such substandard homes. This would not only save money for the citizens affected, but if one adds up the thousands of homes falling within this category it would save the government millions of dollars and many millions of gallons of fuel.
Probably I should not even say this, Mr. Speaker, but I feel very strongly that the residential rehabilitation program is admirable. I give full marks to whoever was responsible for introducing it. But when one experiences the bureaucratic nightmare that exists, one doubts the sincerity that is extended to those to whom the program is directed. Realizing the problems that the minister faces in dealing with provincial and municipal regulations, my main task is to try to impress upon him that every effort should be made and every initiative used to come to an agreement with the provinces concerned, so that this program can be put into effect at the earliest opportunity. I ask the representative of the minister here tonight to reply to me in earnestness on the progress made up until this time to help relieve the burden of low income earners in whatever category they happen to fall.

whenever possible, the best form of agreement to facilitate program flexibility, and the establishment of a federal-provincial committee to co-ordinate the total activity of the program.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-THREAT OF GRASSHOPPER INFESTATION IN WESTERN CANADA THIS SPRING-ACTION TO CONTROL
speechtext:
I rise tonight to expand on the question I asked of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) several weeks ago concerning any controls the minister may have in mind for dealing with the potential outbreak of grasshopper infestation which this year could destroy a major portion of the crops in western Canada. When I raised this matter which is of concern to my constituents, the minister said, as recorded at page 1120 of Hansard for April 3:
-we are offering to the provinces to set up control centres, with equipment and insecticides, and people who are willing to staff these centres, to make sure we are in a better position than we have ever been to control grasshoppers
I am awaiting the response of the hon. member who will reply on behalf of the minister and who has some farm background. I shall be interested to learn details as to how the program for controlling grasshoppers is to be administered across Canada. People in Canada may wonder why grasshoppers should be discussed in the House of Commons. May I point out to those who live in urban areas and have expressed concern about food costs and supplies that Mother Nature has played a dirty trick on us. I am talking of what has happened with regard to food production
Adjournment Debate
within the last four or five years. In the Peace River country wheather conditions have been such that millions of bushels of Durum and hard wheat have been lost. A map showing areas of potential grasshopper infestation will show that we stand to lose further hundreds of millions of bushels of western grain used for bread.
This infestation is not new. When I came to the House in 1971 I told the House that there were was the potential for an outbreak cf the grasshopper plague and that measures should be taken to help affected areas and municipalities fight this outbreak. The outbreak was worse in 1972. It was again worse in 1973. In 1974 we will be faced with a severe situation. I have raised this question with the minister on previous occasions. In spite of opposition from the Conservative Party, the agriculture committee passed a motion that the funds remaining in the old PFAA fund be put into a disaster fund to help fight regional disasters in this country, such as severe outbreaks of grasshoppers. I might point out to the hon. member who will be replying this evening that in the southernmost part of my constituency grasshopper eggs have been hatching at a tremendous rate. Later in the spring we will see the serious results of this hatching. There seems to have been very little winter kill.
Recently I sent a questionnaire to my constituents which was responded to in large numbers. I asked the following question:
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has some funds left in its account in spite of it no long being in total operation. Would you agree with these monies being used to establish an emergency fund to assist with regional disasters such as severe grasshopper infestation?
These funds were collected from farmers in the prairie region; therefore, it was not an easy question in the sense of knowing what the response would be. The response was that 83.5 per cent of the producers in my area said yes, 7 per cent said no, and 9.5 per cent did not know one way or another. I suggest to the government that in the time frame of this year a concerted effort will have to be made to bring this pest under control, otherwise we will stand to lose millions of bushels of wheat and millions of dollars.
There is the long-range question involving the grasshopper problem. It may seem preposterous-and there was great hilarity when I raised this before, including members from western Canada on the agriculture committee, but not from the minister because he knows these studies are taking place-but one aspect of interest to people in the Far East is the fact that the grasshopper is edible. It is a delicacy on the Japanese market. Many people have been critical of me for suggesting that with a long-range program we may be able to avoid all the insecticides and debate about the harmful effects of insecticides. We could use a mechanism to harvest grasshoppers, turning them into a marketable commodity for the Far East.
I want to point out, in the few moments I have left, that I have not gone completely "bonkers" as a result of working too hard in the last couple of weeks. I quote as follows from an article in the Western Producer:

subtopic: POST OFFICE-PROPORTION OF EMPLOYEES WORKING ON MECHANICAL SORTING DEVICES RECRUITED FROM WITHIN SERVICE

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles E. Haliburton (South Western Nova):
subtopic: POST OFFICE-PROPORTION OF EMPLOYEES WORKING ON MECHANICAL SORTING DEVICES RECRUITED FROM WITHIN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question which I directed to the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) on April 1 requesting him to advise us what proportion of code operators had been recruited from within the postal service. At that time it was Your Honour's pleasure to say that it was a question asking for statistics and one which the minister could not be expected to answer during the oral question period. With all due respect to Your Honour, the question was not statistical in one sense, because the answer was "none", and I believe the minister could easily have answered it. Not a single full-time postal employee accepted the offer made to people within the service to operate the machines.
The reason was obvious. They were offered a lower paying job. This has led to one of the most urgent and demoralizing problems within the Post Office. The minister established a new category of employment for code operators. As I understand it, it is the lowest category of all. In spite of repeated evidence of basic union objection to this new and lower classification, in spite of the fact that other countries operating coding machines pay operators more, rather than less, than manual sorters, and in spite of the fact that being a code operator is a much less desirable job because of noise, isolation and boredom, the minister has refused to reconsider his position. He refused to classify code operators as sorters. He refused to have meaningful discussions with the representatives of the employees. He insisted that they be paid 50 cents to 70 cents an hour less. I am not sure of the exact statistics because there are some conflicting figures on this.
I know that the minister was perfectly within his rights. I also know job classification is a matter for management to decide. But it was patently irresponsible for the minister not to read the storm warnings. Morale is low in the Post Office and it is getting lower. The minister did nothing to defuse the power keg; he just put his fingers in his ears and waited for it to blow. And as we all know, it blew.
The minister had one very important way in which he might have eased the tension. He wrote into the collective bargaining agreement of May, 1973, a provision for a manpower committee. I gather it met once or twice some time ago, but the committee spent its time haggling about organizational matters and never did discuss the real problem affecting management and employee relationships. That committee could have provided an excellent opportunity to work out any differences between management and labour, but the minister did not call it.
The people of Canada have now had to pay with a strike, a strike that should never have happened. They have had to pay a heavy price for the arrogance of a minister who looked so promising when he came to his post a couple of years ago. I remember very well, as will many Canadians, his promise at that time that a new day of co-operation and consultation with his employees had dawned. The Canadian public has had to pay the price, Mr. Speaker, and that price, as we all know, is pretty high-millions of
May 2, 1974

dollars of lost mail service and, to add insult to injury, during the strike thousands of dollars spent to advertise the minister's excuses for a strike by his employees.
Canadians are anxious to have an efficient and economic mail service in Canada. Naturally they are angry with the postal workers for their actions of a few weeks ago. Moreover, they are angry with the minister for having failed entirely to deal with the obvious problems with the postal service. The minister represents to the Canadian public that this code sorting system is the answer to all our postal problems. Well, Mr. Speaker, if he could not sell the code, and the jobs it offered, to his own employees, it will be interesting to see how he expects to sell it to the Canadian public.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: POST OFFICE-PROPORTION OF EMPLOYEES WORKING ON MECHANICAL SORTING DEVICES RECRUITED FROM WITHIN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to reply to the question asked tonight by the distinguished member for South Western Nova (Mr. Halibur-ton). The minister would have wished to be here himself, but has gone to Winnipeg tonight to launch a new stamp tomorrow morning. The question that the hon. member raised is, as we all realize, a very important one, and as we all realize relates to the national postal conflict during the last few weeks. The matter is still under study by representatives of the ministry and those of unions under the direction of Mr. Eric Taylor.
Adjournment Debate
If the hon. member would switch on his simultaneous translation, I will give him the balance of the reply tonight.

The Post Office Department has only two highly mechanized offices at the present time, one in Ottawa and the other in Winnipeg. When the automation process is completed, there will be 26 such offices altogether. In the two offices where the mail is sorted automatically, there are 67 coders, 43 of them in Ottawa and the remaining 24 in Winnipeg.
How many coding machine operators are former Post Office employees? Out of the 43 operators working in Ottawa at the present time, 26 were not employed by the Post Office Department, while the remaining 18 were casual or part time employees.
As for Winnipeg, while five coders are former casual or part time employees of the department, the remaining 19 were recruited outside the department.

In closing, Mr. Speaker, the minister has asked me to extend his gratitude to the member for South Western Nova for having last week, when the matter was scheduled to be before the House, abstained from pushing the question. This would have meant possible embarrassment to the minister in his negotiations, and he is most appreciative of the hon. member's patience in this regard.
